evidence: We estimate the prevalence of ADHD among SUD patients at 21%
notes: No CI in abstract.

topic: ADHD among adults in drug and alcohol services
outcome: ADHD in adults attending substance treatment services
evidence: A prevalence rate of 22%, 95% CI [19, 25] was found
notes: 99 estimates. Cannabis users 33% (28-39); women using cocaine 5% (1-11); opioids 27% (20-36) women, 24% (19-30) men. Significant heterogeneity.

topic: Cannabis use disorder in ADHD, lifetime
outcome: lifetime cannabis use disorder among people with ADHD
evidence: lifetime and current prevalence rates of CUD in ADHD populations were 26.9% and 19.2%, respectively
notes: Prediction interval 12.4% to 48.8% (not a CI). Current prevalence 19.2% (prediction interval 5.5%-39.1%). Risk ratio vs general population 2.85 lifetime, 2.91 current.

evidence: The relative risk (RR) for PTSD in ADHD was 2.9 (P < .0005); in samples using healthy controls, the RR was 3.7
notes: No CI in abstract. Comparator dependence: RR 3.7 vs healthy controls, 1.6 vs traumatised controls, not significant vs psychiatric controls. RR for ADHD in PTSD 1.7. 2016 landmark; no newer pooled overall estimate found.

topic: ADHD and PTSD comorbidity: sex difference
evidence: diagnosis of ADHD/PTSD was significantly higher in females than in males (OR = 1.32, p = 0.02)
notes: Fixed-effects model; no CI in abstract. Adults only OR 1.41; structured interview studies OR 1.46. benefit_sign 0: contrast is female vs male.

topic: Adverse childhood experiences and later ADHD
evidence: ACEs were found to be associated with subsequent ADHD (OR = 1.68, 95% CI: 1.54-1.83)
notes: Total n given only as 'nearly 4 million' (not entered). n given as nearly 4 million. Stronger for multiple ACEs and in females. Observational; direction of causation not established.

journal: The International journal of eating disorders
evidence: pooled odds ratio of diagnosing any ED in ADHD was increased significantly, 3.82 (95% CI:2.34-6.24)
notes: Anorexia 4.28 (2.24-8.16), bulimia 5.71 (3.56-9.16), binge eating 4.13 (3-5.67). Rater/method effect: ADHD by clinical interview OR 5.89 (4.32-8.04) vs self-report OR 2.23 (1.23-4.03). ADHD in eating disorder samples OR 2.57 (1.30-5.11). 2016 landmark.

evidence: both children (odds ratio=1.20, 95% CI=1.05-1.37) and adults (odds ratio=1.55, 95% CI=1.32-1.81)
notes: 42 studies and 728,136 individuals in total (children plus adults). Obesity prevalence 28.2% (22.8-34.4) in adults with ADHD vs 16.4% (13.4-19.9) without. Medicated individuals not at higher risk. Held with direct interview and measured height/weight.

evidence: both children (odds ratio=1.20, 95% CI=1.05-1.37) and adults (odds ratio=1.55, 95% CI=1.32-1.81)
notes: Child effect smaller than adult effect (age contrast). Prevalence 10.3% (7.9-13.3) vs 7.4% (5.4-10.1).

topic: Overweight/obesity in children and adolescents with ADHD (update)
evidence: significant risk for co-occurring overweight and obesity [OR 1.56; 95% confidence intervals (CI) 1.32-1.85]
notes: Unmedicated patients OR 1.54 (1.22-1.94); Asia OR 3.25 (1.70-6.21); Europe OR 1.85 (1.61-2.12).

outcome: co-occurring ADHD in the autism population
evidence: 28% (95% CI 25-32) for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder; 20% (17-23) for anxiety disorders
notes: 96 studies in the meta-analyses across 8 conditions. All I2 > 95% (entered as 95). Clinical samples higher than population or registry samples. No meta-analysis of autism prevalence among adults with ADHD was found.

topic: Sleep onset latency in adults with ADHD (actigraphy)
evidence: sleep onset latency: 0.80 (0.46-1.14); sleep efficiency: -0.68 (-1.03, -0.34)
notes: 13 studies in the review. Subjective vs objective split: 7 of 9 subjective parameters differed (SMD 0.56 to 1.55), 2 of 5 actigraphic, 0 polysomnographic.

topic: Sleep efficiency in adults with ADHD (actigraphy)
evidence: sleep onset latency: 0.80 (0.46-1.14); sleep efficiency: -0.68 (-1.03, -0.34)
notes: Negative = lower efficiency in ADHD. No significant polysomnographic differences.

evidence: negative effect of sleep restriction on cognitive processing across cognitive domains (g=-0.383, p<0.001)
notes: Experimental manipulation; 61 studies, 71 populations. No CI in abstract. Moderated by age group, time of day, cumulative days, sex. benefit_sign 0 (not an ADHD contrast); negative = impairment.

evidence: executive functioning (g=-0.324, p<0.001), sustained attention (g=-0.409, p<0.001), and long-term memory (g=-0.192, p=0.002)
notes: Sustained attention is the most affected domain. Size is comparable to many ADHD vs control task differences, so short sleep is a plausible mimic.

evidence: executive functioning (g=-0.324, p<0.001), sustained attention (g=-0.409, p<0.001), and long-term memory (g=-0.192, p=0.002)
notes: No CI in abstract.

topic: One night of sleep restriction: attentional lapses
comparison: sleep restriction (2-6 h) vs normal sleep
evidence: increased reaction times (SMD = 0.512, p < 0.001) and attentional lapses (SMD = 0.489, p < 0.001)
notes: Positive = more lapses. Reaction time SMD 0.512; subjective sleepiness SMD 0.986 (self-rated effect twice the task effect). No effect on working memory, inhibitory control, choice RT. Degree of impairment not related to sleep duration.

topic: Serum ferritin in children with ADHD
evidence: children with ADHD = 1560, HCs = 4691, Hedges' g = -0.246, p = 0.013
notes: 17 articles overall. No difference in serum iron or transferrin. Iron deficiency associated with ADHD OR 1.636 (p = 0.031); symptom severity higher with iron deficiency g = 0.888 (n = 155 only). No CI in abstract.

topic: Serum ferritin in children with ADHD (update)
evidence: pooled mean difference (MD) in serum ferritin levels between children with ADHD and healthy controls was -9.74 (95% CI: -16.50, -2.98)
notes: Raw mean difference (units as in source, presumably ng/mL), not an SMD. Small-study effect: <199 participants MD -12.12 (-21.91, -2.34) vs >=200 MD -7.64 (-17.33, 2.05, not significant). Rises with year: before 2015 MD -1.94, after 2016 -19.43. Case-control -1.95 vs cross-sectional -14.85. North America -1.42 (n.s.). No adult meta-analysis found.

topic: Vitamin D levels in children with ADHD
outcome: serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D, weighted mean difference ng/mL
evidence: weighted mean difference: -6.75 ng/mL; 95% CI: -9.73, -3.77 ng/mL; I2 = 94.9%
notes: Low vitamin D status and ADHD OR 2.57 (1.09-6.04), I2 84.3%, 5 studies. Perinatal low vitamin D RR 1.40 (1.09-1.81), sensitive to one study. Authors call the association equivocal. Children only.

topic: Pre-injury ADHD in children with traumatic brain injury
evidence: rate of pre-TBI ADHD diagnoses was 16.0% (95% CrI, 11.3%-21.7%)
notes: Bayesian credible intervals. General paediatric comparison 10.8% (10.2-11.4). ADHD precedes injury as well as following it.

topic: ADHD after severe traumatic brain injury
comparison: severe TBI vs uninjured controls, more than 1 year
evidence: noninjured controls (≤1 year: OR, 2.62; 95% CrI, 0.76-6.64; >1 year: OR, 6.25; 95% CrI, 2.06-15.06)
notes: Dose-response by severity: concussion OR 0.32 (0.05-1.13) and mild TBI >1 year OR 1.07 (0.35-2.48) are null; moderate >1 year OR 3.67 (0.83-10.56). 35.5% (20.6-53.2) of severe TBI had ADHD after 1 year. Children only; no adult meta-analysis found.

evidence: pooled prevalence of ADHD in epilepsy was 22.3% (95% CI 20.3-24.4%)
notes: k and n for the whole meta-analysis. Heterogeneity attributed partly to sample size and diagnostic method.

evidence: the pooled prevalence of epilepsy in ADHD was 3.4% (95% CI 2.53-4.21%)
notes: Asymmetric comorbidity: 22.3% one way, 3.4% the other.

outcome: objective cognitive performance incl. attention and executive functioning
evidence: Across 102 articles, N =  3,943 participants, and 730 comparisons, we observe no systematic robust evidence for significant cycle shifts
notes: Null result; no single pooled g in abstract. No publication bias or small-study effects. Not an ADHD sample: no meta-analysis of cycle phase and ADHD symptoms exists.

evidence: perimenopausal women exhibited poorer cognitive outcomes than premenopausal women (moderate effect)
notes: No number in abstract (described as moderate); es null, full text not open access. Effect only in studies using STRAW+10 staging. Versus postmenopause: better objective outcomes but a trend to poorer self-reported outcomes (subjective/objective dissociation). n = total across 26 articles.

comparison: correlation of self-reported with tested cognition
journal: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society : JINS
evidence: subjective cognition and objective measures of learning efficiency (r = .12; CI = .02 to .23)
notes: Other domains non-significant. Self-reported 'brain fog' barely tracks tested performance. 24 studies, 5629 participants in the review; 6 in the meta-analysis.

topic: Adult ADHD prevalence by sex: men (persistent)
notes: Full text: https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7916320 (subgroup table). Sex ratio in adult population surveys is close to 1:1: men 4.99% vs women 4.49%, subgroup p = 0.70. Symptomatic ADHD: men 8.05% (6.1-10.23) vs women 7.76% (5.79-9.98), p = 0.85. Crude pooled values exceed the age-standardised 2.58%.

topic: Adult ADHD prevalence by sex: women (persistent)
notes: Full text: https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC7916320 (subgroup table). No meta-analysis of the male-to-female diagnosis ratio in adults was found; this subgroup contrast is the nearest pooled evidence. Tool effect in the same table: ASRS 5.95% (3.52-8.95) vs other tools 3.71% (2.32-5.39).

topic: ADHD prevalence by study type: registers
journal: European psychiatry : the journal of the Association of European Psychiatrists
evidence: prevalence of ADHD in register studies was 1.6%, 95% CI [0.9; 3.0], in survey studies 5.0%, 95% CI [2.9; 8.6]
notes: 103 studies, 159 datapoints across all study types. Surveys give about three times the register figure. One-stage clinical 4.2% [2.9; 6.0], two-stage clinical 4.8% [4.0; 5.8].

topic: ADHD prevalence by study type: surveys
journal: European psychiatry : the journal of the Association of European Psychiatrists
evidence: prevalence of ADHD in register studies was 1.6%, 95% CI [0.9; 3.0], in survey studies 5.0%, 95% CI [2.9; 8.6]
notes: Ascertainment method drives the estimate (register 1.6 vs survey 5.0).

topic: Proportion of diagnosed ADHD treated with medication
outcome: pharmacological treatment among people with clinically confirmed ADHD
evidence: pooled prevalence of pharmacologically treated ADHD was 73.4% (95% CI: 63.4-81.5)
notes: 95% prediction interval 29.6%-94.5%; extremely high heterogeneity; authors say not for clinical inference. No sex difference.

topic: Trend in ADHD medication consumption, 64 countries
outcome: ADHD medication consumption (DDD per 1000 inhabitants aged 5-19 per day), % change per year
evidence: consumption increased by +9.72% (95% confidence interval [CI], +6.25%, +13.31%) per year, from 1.19 DDD/TID in 2015 to 1.43
notes: No meta-analysis of prescribing trends found; multinational sales-data study. Increase in high-income countries only: 6.39 DDD/TID (4.63-8.84) high income vs 0.37 upper-middle vs 0.02 lower-middle in 2019.

topic: Trend in ADHD medication use, adults, 13 countries
outcome: prevalence of any ADHD medication use in adults aged 19+
evidence: absolute increase in ADHD medication use prevalence per year ranged from 0·0006% to 0·12%
notes: No pooled figure; es null. Adult use in 2010 ranged 0.003% to 1.48% (North America 1.42%, northern Europe 0.47%, western Europe 0.03%, Asia and Australia 0.05%). Rose in all countries. n = 154.5 million across all ages. Abstract prints decimals with a middle dot.

topic: Trend in ADHD diagnosis: overdiagnosis evidence
outcome: evidence that diagnosis and treatment have increased
evidence: Evidence that actual ADHD diagnosis had increased was found in 45 studies (question 2)
notes: Systematic scoping review, no pooled estimate. 83 studies showed rising pharmacological treatment; 25 suggested added cases are milder; only 5 studied benefit vs harm in milder cases. Children and adolescents only. By contrast clinical-setting prevalence showed no time trend 1981-2023 (PMID 40877470).

topic: Relative-age effect: ADHD diagnosis (largest pooled sample)
comparison: youngest third vs older in school year
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: summarized relative risk of an ADHD diagnosis was 1.34 (95% CI, 1.26-1.43, p < .001)
notes: 164,049 ADHD cases. Very high heterogeneity. Agrees with the 2025 review (RR 1.38).

topic: Adult ADHD self-report scales (ASRS, CAARS and others): accuracy
outcome: positive and negative predictive value of self-report screening scales
evidence: At best, positive predictive values in clinical samples reached 61%, but most fell below 20%
notes: Systematic review, not pooled; es null. Negative predictive values exceeded 96%, so scales rule out well and rule in poorly. No meta-analysis of ASRS or CAARS sensitivity/specificity in adults was found.
No systematic review or meta-analysis of DIVA accuracy was returned by any search (ASRS/DIVA/CAARS title and abstract queries). Gap.

topic: ADHD screening tools in children: overall accuracy
outcome: area under the curve, combined ADHD symptom score
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: pooled AUC for studies using a combined ADHD symptoms score was 0.82 (95% CI = 0.78-0.86)
notes: Rater effect: AUC varied across reporters 0.67-0.92. No measure met 0.8 sensitivity and 0.8 specificity together. k = 75 studies, 41 tools. Child data, given because the adult equivalent does not exist.

topic: Child rating scale accuracy: CBCL attention problems
evidence: pooled sensitivities of 0.77, 0.75, 0.72, and 0.83 and pooled specificities of 0.73, 0.75, 0.84, and 0.84
notes: Specificity 0.73. Conners parent 0.75/0.75, Conners teacher 0.72/0.84, Conners ASQ 0.83/0.84 (11 articles). No CI in abstract.

evidence: PVTs (stand-alone and embedded) produced a large effect size (g = 0.84, 95% confidence interval [CI; 0.72, 1.13]
notes: College-student simulation designs only. Stand-alone PVTs g = 0.98 [0.84, 1.12] beat embedded g = 0.66 [0.51, 0.80]. CI as printed (asymmetric around 0.84).

evidence: overall SVTs (stand-alone and embedded) produced a medium-effect size (g = 0.54, 95% CI [0.44, 0.65]
notes: Self-report validity scales detect feigning less well than performance tests (0.54 vs 0.84): objective beats self-report.

topic: Feigned ADHD: continuous performance tests as validity indicators
evidence: CPTs effectively distinguish between credible and noncredible performance (g = 0.73)
notes: Design effect: simulation studies g = 0.94 vs criterion-group (real clinical) studies g = 0.55. 67 effect sizes. No CI in abstract.

outcome: proportion of adult ADHD diagnoses that are wrong (false positive or false negative)
notes: No meta-analysis of misdiagnosis rates found (title searches for misdiagnosis/overdiagnosis/underdiagnosis returned 0 reviews; abstract search returned no pooled estimate). Nearest evidence: screen-positive vs two-stage prevalence (26.7% vs 14.61%, PMID 35373645) and low positive predictive value of scales (PMID 37366274).

outcome: executive function, more than 4 weeks after infection
evidence: executive function (standardised mean difference (SMD) -0.45), learning and memory (SMD -0.55), complex attention (SMD -0.54)
notes: High-quality studies only (>40 participants, healthy controls). No CI in abstract. Broad, not domain-specific: language -0.54, perceptual motor -0.70. A correction was published (PMID 40539250). benefit_sign 0; negative = impairment.

outcome: complex attention, more than 4 weeks after infection
evidence: executive function (standardised mean difference (SMD) -0.45), learning and memory (SMD -0.55), complex attention (SMD -0.54)
notes: Attention deficit after COVID is of the size typically reported for ADHD vs controls on tasks, so it is a credible mimic. Heterogeneous tasks and severities.

outcome: self-reported concentration impairment at 6 months or more
evidence: concentration impairment 23.8% (95% CI [17.2-31.9%])
notes: Cognitive impairment 27.1% [20.4-34.9], memory disorders 27.8% [20.1-37.1], fatigue 43.3% [36.1-50.9], sleep disorders 24.4% [18.1-32.1]. Over 4 million patients; significant heterogeneity for all symptoms.

topic: Long COVID: mental health conditions and brain fog
outcome: combined prevalence of mental health conditions and brain fog, 3-24 months
evidence: combined prevalence of mental health conditions and brain fog was 20·4% (95% CI 11·1%-34·4%)
notes: Abstract prints decimals with a middle dot. Community-managed 29.7% vs hospitalised 19.5%. Odds rose over time and when validated instruments were used; fell with vaccination.

topic: Long COVID brain fog: tested cognition
evidence: significantly lower cognitive performance (Hedge's g=-0.63, 95% CI -1.15 to -0.12)
notes: I2 > 70% (entered as 70). Fatigue g = 2.64 (0.41 to 4.86) and depressive symptoms g = 1.48 (0.40 to 2.55) are far larger than the tested cognitive deficit: self-rated state dominates over objective performance.

outcome: explained common variance by the general factor, %
journal: Clinical child and family psychology review
evidence: general psychopathology explained over half (~ 56%) of the reliable variance in symptoms of psychopathology
notes: 110 effect sizes (ECV). Stable across age. Approximate value, no CI in abstract. No adult-specific meta-analysis of p-factor strength found.

topic: HiTOP structure: fit of five transdiagnostic dimensions
outcome: comparative fit index of a five-dimension model of DSM diagnoses
evidence: Five transdiagnostic dimensions fit the DSM diagnoses well (comparative fit index = 0.92, root mean square error of approximation = 0.07
notes: Meta-analytic factor analysis of a pooled correlation matrix. RMSEA 0.07, SRMR 0.03. Most diagnoses loaded > |0.30| on expected factors.

topic: HiTOP with cognition: general factor loadings
outcome: loading of eight disorders and seven cognitive functions on a general factor (median)
journal: Perspectives on psychological science : a journal of the Association for Psychological Science
evidence: general factor with strong loadings of all disorders and cognitive functions (median λ = |.51|, range = |.30| to |.64|)
notes: ci_low/ci_high hold the RANGE of loadings, not a confidence interval. Pooled three published meta-analyses. Cognitive dysfunction loads on the same general factor as diagnoses.

comparison: patients vs controls across 12 disorder categories
evidence: all disorders reviewed are associated with underperformance across cognitive domains
notes: Review of meta-analyses: 97 clinical samples, 1,055 effect sizes; no single pooled number in abstract, es null. Authors argue motivation and emotion contribute to test underperformance. An antisaccade meta-analysis (PMID 39103067; k = 146, n = 13,807) likewise finds inhibitory deficits across disorders, largest in schizophrenia.

topic: Subjective vs objective cognition across conditions
comparison: correlation of self-reported with tested cognition
evidence: pooled correlation between overall objective and subjective cognition was 0.14 (95 % CI [0.08, 0.21]
notes: k = 10 reviews (second-order meta-analysis); under 2% shared variance. Depression and anxiety relate to self-reported cognition more strongly than test scores do. Matches the menopause result (r = .12).

topic: Genetic correlation: ADHD with other psychiatric symptoms
outcome: pooled rg between ADHD and other psychiatric symptoms
journal: Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines
evidence: pooled genetic correlation of 0.50, 95% confidence interval: 0.46-0.60
notes: Metric is rg. Similar for externalizing .49 [0.37-0.61], internalizing .50 [0.39-0.69], neurodevelopmental .56 [0.47-0.66]: no specificity by disorder family.

topic: Genetic correlation: ADHD with other symptoms, childhood
outcome: rg between ADHD and other psychiatric symptoms
journal: Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines
evidence: genetic correlations in childhood and adulthood were rg  = .53 (0.43-0.63) and rg  = .51 (0.44-0.56), respectively
notes: Metric is rg. No child/adult difference.

topic: Genetic correlation: ADHD with other symptoms, adulthood
outcome: rg between ADHD and other psychiatric symptoms
journal: Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines
evidence: genetic correlations in childhood and adulthood were rg  = .53 (0.43-0.63) and rg  = .51 (0.44-0.56), respectively
notes: Metric is rg. Rater did not matter here: self-report .52 (0.47-0.58), other informants .55 (0.41-0.69), combined .50 (0.33-0.65).

topic: Genetic overlap: ADHD variants shared with other disorders
outcome: proportion of ADHD-influencing common variants shared with other psychiatric disorders, %
evidence: 84-98% of ADHD-influencing variants are shared with other psychiatric disorders
notes: Range only (84-98%), es null. GWAS meta-analysis, 38,691 ADHD and 186,843 controls. Disorder-pair rg values (SNP-based) are in the full text, which the Europe PMC full-text service did not return in this session; the eight-disorder cross-disorder analysis (PMID 31835028) also gives no rg in its abstract.

evidence: Insomnia was far more frequent among adults with ADHD (66.8%) than in the population controls (28.8%)
notes: No meta-analysis of insomnia prevalence in adult ADHD found. 268 ADHD, 202 controls. Combined presentation 79.7% vs inattentive 55.6%. Current stimulant users had lower insomnia scores.

topic: Restless legs syndrome in adults with ADHD
outcome: restless legs syndrome by standard criteria
evidence: RLS was diagnosed in 33.0%, associated with earlier onset of ADHD
notes: No meta-analysis in adults found (a 2025 paediatric systematic review exists, PMID 40981213, not pooled here). Iron deficiency (ferritin < 50 ng/mL) in 35.5%, more often with RLS. Periodic limb movement index did not differ from controls. 200 adults with ADHD (112 men).

topic: Obstructive sleep apnoea in children with ADHD
certainty: GRADE applied; rating not stated in abstract
evidence: pooled prevalence of OSA in children with ADHD was 44% (  95% CI [2%, 56%])
notes: CI as printed in the abstract (lower bound 2% looks like a typo). Children only; no adult meta-analysis found. Adenotonsillectomy improved ADHD symptoms (descriptive).

topic: Delayed sleep phase / circadian rhythm in ADHD
outcome: delayed sleep phase prevalence, chronotype, melatonin onset
notes: No meta-analysis found (query on chronotype/eveningness/delayed sleep/circadian with ADHD returned 0 meta-analyses). Systematic reviews without pooling exist (PMID 28064405, 2017; PMID 33402013, 2022).

topic: Thyroid hormones in children with neurodevelopmental disorders
evidence: thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) (SMD = -0.22; 95% CI = -0.41 to -0.03; pES = 0.026)
notes: Pooled across neurodevelopmental disorders; authors state changes were mainly in ADHD. FT4 SMD -0.67 (-0.69 to -0.64, implausibly narrow), TT4 -0.35 (-0.50 to -0.20), FT3 0.22 (0.04 to 0.40). 54 studies overall. No meta-analysis of thyroid dysfunction in adults with ADHD, or of thyroid disease presenting as ADHD, was found.

topic: Sex hormones and ADHD symptoms in females
outcome: ADHD symptoms across puberty, menstrual cycle, pregnancy
evidence: A total of 11 studies were included in this review
notes: Systematic review, narrative only; no pooled estimate. Suggestive of symptom change across the cycle and puberty; small heterogeneous studies. No studies on menopause or perimenopause and ADHD symptoms; no pooled evidence on oestrogen and ADHD.

topic: Learning disorders / dyslexia co-occurring with ADHD
outcome: specific learning disorder or dyslexia among people with ADHD
notes: No meta-analysis of co-occurrence rates found in three searches (title and abstract terms for dyslexia, reading disorder, learning disorder with ADHD). Only neuroimaging and treatment meta-analyses were returned.

outcome: autism spectrum disorder among adults with ADHD
notes: No meta-analysis of autism prevalence in ADHD samples found; pooled evidence exists only in the other direction (ADHD in 28% of autistic people, PMID 31447415).

journal: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging
evidence: a statistically significant difference of medium magnitude effect size was present for the case-control comparisons (d=0.43; p < 10-15)
notes: k = 25 case-control comparisons from 21 investigations. Abstract: no significant differences by sample age (child vs adult), reward outcome (real vs hypothetical) or CD/ODD comorbidity; minimal heterogeneity and minimal evidence of publication bias; meta-regression on publication year run. Positive = steeper discounting in ADHD.

topic: Choice impulsivity (delay discounting + delay of gratification), children
evidence: Results revealed a medium-magnitude between-group effect size (g=.47), suggesting that children and adolescents with ADHD exhibited moderately increased impulsive decision-making
notes: 28 tasks from 26 studies (ADHD 2360, TD 1960). Similar effects across delay discounting and delay of gratification tasks. Single-informant diagnosis gave larger effects than multi-informant; samples excluding females gave larger effects.

topic: Delay aversion: simple choice-delay vs temporal discounting; real vs hypothetical rewards
outcome: choice of small immediate over large delayed reward
evidence: Moderation analyses show that offering real rewards in the SCP almost doubled the odds ratio for participants with ADHD
notes: Pooled ORs not given in abstract (not open access), so es is null. 37 group comparisons (22 simple choice paradigm, 15 temporal discounting), 3,763 participants (53% ADHD); small-to-medium effects in both paradigms. Incentive finding: real rewards almost doubled the OR in the simple choice paradigm. This conflicts with Jackson 2016 (no real vs hypothetical difference in discounting tasks).

evidence: Meta-analysis showed a significant medium effect size (Cohen's d=0.48-0.58) in terms of ventral-striatal (VS)-hyporesponsiveness in ADHD
notes: Pre-2015 landmark kept as the reference: no later ADHD meta-analysis with a pooled ventral striatal effect size was found. Abstract reports a range, d = 0.48 to 0.58; lower bound entered. Positive = lower VS activation in ADHD. In healthy samples trait impulsivity correlates positively with VS activation (opposite direction). Authors state the number of studies is small. k and n not in abstract.

topic: Reward receipt (hedonic) processing, fMRI, ADHD and autism
evidence: Our coordinate-based meta-analysis of 29 studies (468 ADHD patients, 424 ASD patients, and 1027 healthy controls, HCs)
notes: Coordinate-based meta-analysis: no standardized pooled effect size, so es is null. n = 468 ADHD + 424 ASD + 1027 controls across both disorders. Shared abnormal putamen and amygdala activation in ADHD and ASD; disorder-specific differences in prefrontal cortex. Pre-registered. Most recent reward fMRI meta-analysis for ADHD found.

topic: Effect of reward incentives on inhibitory control (ADHD subgroup tested as moderator)
evidence: The prospect of reward for successful inhibition significantly improved IC (SMD = 0.429, 95% CI = 0.288, 0.570, I2 = 96.7%)
notes: 73 articles, 80 studies; mostly within-subject designs, not RCTs of treatment. No moderation by clinical vs healthy sample. Full text (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8392762): ADHD samples vs healthy controls, no evidence of moderation, chi2(1) = 0.210, p = .646. So incentives improve inhibition about equally in ADHD and controls; the pooled data do not show a larger incentive gain in ADHD. Very high heterogeneity.

evidence: Striatal dopamine transporter density was 14% higher on average in the ADHD group than in the healthy comparison group
notes: Metric is percent difference, not a standardized effect. Pre-2015 landmark; no newer PET/SPECT meta-analysis in ADHD found. 9 studies (169 ADHD, 173 controls). Heterogeneity large and significant. Medication history: meta-regression showed density higher in previously medicated patients and lower in drug-naive patients, so the direction of the group difference depends on stimulant exposure. No moderation by age, year or imaging technique; no publication bias detected.

topic: Dopamine D2/D3 receptor availability and dopamine release (PET)
evidence: No meta-analysis located in searches q3, q5, q9, q28, q39
notes: Gap. Searches returned only genetic-association meta-analyses (DRD4, SLC6A3 VNTR) and the 2012 dopamine transporter meta-analysis. No pooled PET estimate for D2/D3 receptors or stimulus-evoked dopamine release in ADHD was found. The evidence field is the extractor's statement, not a quotation.

topic: Effort discounting vs delay discounting, adolescents
evidence: adolescents with ADHD showed steeper discounting than controls for DD, but not for ED
notes: No meta-analysis of effort discounting in ADHD exists; a 2024 scoping review (Wagner, PMID 38895497) found only 12 studies with mixed results. This study: 30 ADHD, 28 controls, age 12-17; group difference for delay but not physical effort. A second small study (Chong 2023, PMID 37666665; 20 ADHD, 24 controls) found the opposite: lower willingness to invest cognitive and physical effort off medication, restored by amphetamine. No effect size in either abstract.

comparison: correlation with ADHD symptoms or diagnosis
journal: Clinical Child and Family Psychology Review
evidence: Across 18 mostly correlational studies (total N = 22,365), an overall effect of r = 0.40 (95% CI: 0.35-0.46) was observed
notes: Mostly cross-sectional questionnaire studies, so shared method variance is likely (rater not stated in abstract; entered as self). Closest pooled evidence to the motivation / interest-based attention topic.

comparison: ADHD vs psychiatric outpatients without ADHD
evidence: Adolescents with ADHD reported significantly higher MWQ scores than those without ADHD (p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.92)
notes: No meta-analysis of mind wandering in ADHD found (q7, q21, q31, q36). A 2021 systematic review (Lanier, PMID 31364436) included 9 studies and did not pool. This is the largest comparative study located: 137 ADHD vs 303 non-ADHD outpatients aged 10-19, retrospective, self-report; difference remained after adjusting for depression and autistic traits (eta2 = 0.098).

evidence: Our sample of 824 effect sizes showed a mean g of 0.688 that was moderated by the age of the sample and working memory

topic: Time perception precision, children and adolescents
evidence: perceived time less accurately (Hedges' g > 0.40), less precisely (Hedges' g = 0.66) and had higher tendency to overestimate time
notes: 1620 ADHD, 1249 controls. Accuracy g > 0.40 (exact value not given) vs precision g = 0.66: the variability measure is larger than the level measure. Not moderated by task type or stimulus modality; moderated by age and gender.

topic: Perceptual timing: discrimination, estimation, production, reproduction
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: From 2,266 records, 55 studies were retained and meta-analyzed with random effects models
notes: Pooled values not in abstract (not open access), es null. Deficits in sub-second discrimination, more variable estimation of multi-second durations, estimation and production pattern read as a faster internal clock; reproduction deficits attributed to attention at short intervals and delay aversion at long intervals.

topic: Discontinuing vs continuing medication: quality of life, children

notes: Tsujii 2020: no detectable QoL loss in adults after discontinuation (wide CI).

evidence: pharmacological treatment options for parent (SMD = 0.67, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.74)

evidence: and teacher ADHD symptom ratings (SMD = 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.82)
notes: Turk 2023; see parent row.

evidence: significant benefits of CBT for core ADHD symptoms (SMD = -0.45, P < 0.00001)

journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
evidence: self-reported ADHD symptoms (SMD -0.84, 95% CI -1.18 to -0.50; 5 studies, 251 participants; moderate-quality evidence

journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
evidence: clinician-reported core symptoms (SMD -0.80, 95% CI -1.31 to -0.30; 2 studies, 65 participants; very low-quality evidence

evidence: superior to waiting list with a moderate to large effect size (standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.76, 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.21, 1.31]

evidence: superior to active control groups with a small to moderate effect size (SMD = 0.43, 95% CI [0.14, 0.71]

journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology
evidence: small-to-medium effects versus control (g = .65; 95% CI [0.44, 0.86] for symptoms

certainty: CINeMA very low to moderate across network
evidence: Cognitive behavioural therapy (-0·76, -1·26 to -0·26)

Abstract: non-drug therapies 'were better than placebo only on clinician-reported measures', not on self-report; 'effects of non-pharmacological strategies were inconsistent across different raters'. 113 RCTs, 14,887 participants in whole network; 28 psychological RCTs (1,116 participants). Stimulants for comparison: self -0.39, clinician -0.61.

evidence: clinician rated: methylphenidate, 0.50, 0.39 to 0.61, evidence certainty moderate; cognitive behavioural therapy, 0.53, 0.29 to 0.77, evidence certainty moderate
notes: Full text: https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12651917 . Umbrella review of 221 re-estimated meta-analyses. CBT is the only non-drug treatment in adults with at least moderate certainty; its clinician-rated effect is the same size as methylphenidate's (0.50). 'No high certainty, long term evidence was found for any intervention.'

evidence: DBT moderately reduced ADHD symptoms (SMD = -0.51 [-0.76, -0.25])
notes: Rater not stated in abstract. Controls were standard treatment, placebo or waitlist, pooled together. Quality of life SMD 0.41 (0.15-0.66). Follow-up data for 533 of 850.

evidence: self-reported ADHD symptoms (SMD = 0.48, 95% CI [0.19, 0.76])
notes: 10 controlled studies in review, not all randomised ('regardless of randomization'); k per outcome not in abstract. Pair with observer-rated row (0.32).

evidence: observer-rated ADHD symptoms (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.09, 0.56])
notes: Observer-rated (abstract does not say whether observers were blind); coded 'clinician'. Observer effect is two thirds of the self-report effect (0.48). Not all studies randomised. Oliva 2021 (PMID 34146899, no pooled number in abstract) reports a gap between medium/large effects in inactive-controlled and low/negligible effects in active-controlled mindfulness studies, plus publication bias.

certainty: CINeMA very low to moderate across network
evidence: mindfulness (-0·79, -1·29 to -0·29)
notes: Mid-dot decimals in source. Better than placebo only on clinician-reported, not self-reported, scales. Gosling 2025 umbrella review (full text): mindfulness in adults 'apparently large' effect (SMD > 0.65) but low or very low certainty.

k = total RCTs in the meta-analysis. Very high heterogeneity (I2 91%) and publication bias not excluded. Rater not stated. Executive function SMD 0.45 (0.02-0.88), I2 84%. Earlier review Lee 2022 (PMID 36429915): g = 0.77, 11 studies, no CI in abstract. Oliva 2021: no active-controlled mindfulness trials in children.

topic: Meditation-based mind-body interventions (mindfulness, yoga, tai chi, qigong)
evidence: positive and small effect on inattention (g = -0.26), hyperactivity/impulsivity (g = -0.19), and EF (g = -0.35)
notes: No CI or k in abstract. RCT-only pooling gives much smaller effects than mindfulness-specific reviews that mix designs.

certainty: CINeMA very low to moderate across network

Dekkers 2022 (PMID 34224837): higher dose of psychoeducation within parent training was negatively related to parental outcomes.

evidence: teacher- and parent-rated symptoms of inattention were g=0.26 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.52) and g=0.56 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.74), respectively
notes: k and n are review totals (12 studies, 1054 children). Parent (proximal) rating. Organisational skills themselves: parent g = 0.83 (0.32-1.34), teacher g = 0.54 (0.17-0.91). GPA g = 0.29 (0.07-0.51).

evidence: teacher- and parent-rated symptoms of inattention were g=0.26 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.52) and g=0.56 (95% CI 0.38 to 0.74), respectively
notes: Teacher rating is under half the parent rating (0.56) in the same trials. k and n are review totals.

No meta-analysis of ADHD coaching found in searches E02 and E16 (title terms 'coaching'). Hits were single uncontrolled or college-student studies (e.g. Prevatt 2015, PMID 23509112; Ahmann 2026, PMID 41909194) and a 2026 survey of US coaching practice (PMID 41538184). Organisational strategies as a CBT component: Matsumoto 2024 (PMID 39732478) incremental OR 2.03 (1.27-3.24) for treatment response.

outcome: Treatment response on ADHD core symptoms
evidence: organisational strategies (incremental OR (iOR)=2.03, 95% CI 1.27 to 3.24)

evidence: showed no significant improvement with neurofeedback (k = 20; n = 1214; SMD, 0.04; 95% CI, -0.10 to 0.18)

evidence: restricted to RCTs using established standard protocols (k = 9; n = 681; SMD, 0.21; 95% CI, 0.02 to 0.40)
notes: Probably blinded raters. Small but significant when restricted to standard protocols.

evidence: only for processing speed (k = 15; n = 909; SMD, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.01 to 0.69)
notes: The only one of 5 neuropsychological outcomes that was significant. Full text: at longer-term follow-up processing speed k = 8, n = 517, SMD 0.32 (0.04-0.61), with significant heterogeneity.

journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: ADHD total symptoms = 0.35, 95% CI = 0.11-0.59; inattention = 0.36, 95% CI = 0.09-0.63
notes: European ADHD Guidelines Group 2016. Most proximal (least blinded) raters. k and n are review totals. Pair with the blinded row from the same review.

journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: Effects were not significant when probably blinded ratings were the outcome or in trials with active/sham controls

evidence: advantage of NF over non-active controls [inattention (post: SMD = 0.38; FU: SMD = 0.57)
notes: Parent (unblinded) ratings only; no CI in abstract. n = 256 NF + 250 control. Hyperactivity-impulsivity post 0.25, follow-up 0.39. Conflicts with Westwood 2025 (blinded raters: no effect at 6-12 months). Active treatments (mainly methylphenidate) beat NF on inattention at post (SMD -0.44).

evidence: ADHD symptoms combined: SMD=-0.578, 95% CI (-1.063 to -0.092)
notes: Negative = methylphenidate better than neurofeedback. 13 of 18 trials Chinese-language. Abstract: 'removing Chinese studies and non-funded studies, no differences emerged'. Dropout lower with NF (OR 0.412, 0.186-0.913). Results at follow-up inconsistent across raters.

Mean age 23.5 (range 6-60), self-report. At 6-12 month follow-up total score SMD 0.22 (-0.08 to 0.52). Courreges 2025 (PMID 40505983; adults, 18 articles): 'meta-analysis did not reach significance for any of the techniques studied' (neurofeedback, tDCS, rTMS).

comparison: neurofeedback vs waitlist / treatment as usual

notes: Waitlist/TAU subgroup: effect appears only against inactive controls (all comparators: inattention SMD -0.11, -0.39 to 0.18). Hyperactivity/impulsivity vs waitlist -0.03 (ns).

evidence: showed no effect on ADHD total (SMD = 0.12, 95%CI[-0.01 to -0.25])

evidence: small improvement in inattention symptoms (SMD = 0.17, 95%CI[0.02-0.31])

evidence: CCT improved WM (verbal: n = 15, SMD = 0.38, 95%CI[0.24-0.53]
notes: Near transfer only: visual-spatial WM SMD 0.49 (0.31-0.67), k = 9; no effect on attention, inhibition, reading or arithmetic. Some persistence of verbal WM at about 6 months (5-7 trials).

journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: total ADHD (standardized mean difference [SMD] = 0.37, 95% CI = 0.09-0.66)
notes: European ADHD Guidelines Group 2015. Most proximal raters; k and n are review totals. Multi-process training, proximal raters: SMD 0.79 (0.46-1.12).

journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: provided by probably blinded raters (ADHD total: SMD = 0.20, 95% CI = 0.01-0.40
notes: Probably blinded estimate is about half the proximal one (0.37). k and n are review totals. 2023 update (Westwood) blinded estimate 0.12. Zulauf-McCurdy 2023 (PMID 37084312), probably blind outcomes only: cognitive training SMD = 0.216, p = 0.032, the only complementary/alternative treatment with overall efficacy.
Adults. 'neither symptom severity nor specific cognitive outcomes (executive functioning, cognitive speed, or working memory) showed a significant improvement'.

evidence: (standard mean difference (SMD) 0.28, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.14-0.41; SMD 0.21, 95% CI 0.03-0.39, respectively)

evidence: (standard mean difference (SMD) 0.28, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.14-0.41; SMD 0.21, 95% CI 0.03-0.39, respectively)

evidence: significant decrease in overall ADHD symptoms (SMD = -0.33; 95 % CI = [-0.51, -0.16])

evidence: no significant improvement in clinical symptoms (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.012, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.235 to 0.259)

evidence: inhibitory control (SMD 0.222, 95% CI 0.045 to 0.399)
notes: Attention SMD 0.207 (0.011-0.403); processing speed 0.063 (ns). Task effects without symptom effects.

notes: Mid-dot decimals in source. Better than placebo on clinician-reported scales only. Neurostimulation and neurofeedback: 10 RCTs, 194 participants in the network.

journal: Revista brasileira de psiquiatria (Sao Paulo, Brazil : 1999)
evidence: no difference in overall ADHD symptoms between those treated with rTMS and sham controls (SMD = -0.24, p = 0.17)

topic: Non-invasive brain stimulation (rTMS, tDCS, TNS), double-blind trials

evidence: estimated adjusted mean difference = 0.83; 95% confidence interval: -2.47 to 4.13; P = 0.622; Cohen's d = 0.09

journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: ADHD-RS total scores showed significant group-by-time interactions (F1,228 = 8.12, p = .005; week 4 Cohen d = 0.5)

evidence: small beneficial effect on overall core symptoms (standardized mean difference [SMD] = -0.39, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.64 to -0.14)

evidence: moderately beneficial effect on overall EFs (SMD = -0.68, 95% CI: -0.91 to -0.45)

evidence: small effect on total ADHD core symptoms (n = 11; g = -0.33; 95% CI [-0.63; -0.02]; p = .037)
notes: Clinically diagnosed samples, RCTs only. Agrees with Huang 2023 (-0.39).

evidence: improving inattention (G = 0.92, 95% CI: 0.44-1.39, 95%)

evidence: small beneficial effect on core symptoms (Hedges' g = 0.23, 95% CI [0.03, 0.43], p = 0.024)

8 articles / 14 studies / 373 participants in whole review; k for chronic subgroup not given. No pooled estimate for symptoms after chronic exercise in adults was found.

topic: Mind-body exercise (yoga, tai chi and similar)
evidence: significantly improved attention in individuals with ADHD [SMD=-0.97, 95% CI (-1.56, -0.39), P < 0.05]

evidence: The FFD ESs were 0.80 (95% CI: 0.41-1.19, I2 = 61%) [parent ratings] and 0.51 (95% CI: -0.02-1.04, I2 = 72%) [other ratings]

evidence: The FFD ESs were 0.80 (95% CI: 0.41-1.19, I2 = 61%) [parent ratings] and 0.51 (95% CI: -0.02-1.04, I2 = 72%) [other ratings]

evidence: 0.08 (95% CI: -0.07-0.24, I2 = 0%) [teacher ratings] and 0.11 (95% CI: -0.13-0.34, I2 = 12%) [observer ratings]

evidence: (standardized mean difference [SMD]: -0.16; 95% CI, -0.34 to 0.01; P = .07)

evidence: ADHD total scores (SMD: -0.62 Hedges' g; 95% CI: -1.24 to -0.002, p = 0.04)

notes: Full text: https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12407005 . 5 vitamin D studies. Gan 2019 (PMID 31368773; 4 RCTs, 256 children, all adjunctive to methylphenidate) reports a 'small but statistically significant improvement' with low to very low quality evidence; no number in abstract.

evidence: multivitamin supplementation did not show a statistically significant effect, with a pooled SMD of –0.01 (95% CI:–1.50 to 1.47)

journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: 54% of the micronutrient and 18% of the placebo group were responders (risk ratio = 2.97, 97.5% CI = 1.50, 5.90, p < .001)

evidence: Nine studies met the eligibility criteria and were selected

evidence: we don't have any predominant evidence about using mineral supplementation on children with ADHD
notes: No meta-analysis of magnesium supplementation found; only meta-analyses of magnesium levels (case-control) exist in the search results.

evidence: Four studies met our inclusion criteria with a total of 118 patients
notes: Systematic review without pooling; 4 small trials, 118 patients in total.

evidence: (standardized mean difference -0.12; 95% CI -0.44 to 0.20; p = 0.45; I2 = 0%)
