evidence: no significant improvement in total symptoms of ADHD (SMD = 0.25; P = 0.12)
notes: No CI in abstract. Adjunct to methylphenidate SMD 0.84 vs stand-alone 0.07 (p = 0.16 for difference).

evidence: probiotic supplementation did not show a clear benefit (SMD = -0.25, 95% CI: -0.57 to 0.07; p = 0.131)
notes: Parent-rated Conners (CPRS) total SMD -0.33 (-0.65 to -0.01) but no effect on SNAP-IV inattention or CPT performance: benefit appears only on the broad parent scale.

certainty: moderate to high (authors' rating for pairwise analysis)
evidence: behavioral sleep [BS] interventions [k = 10]: -0.48 [-0.70, -0.27], p < 0.001
notes: 40 RCTs, 4361 participants in review. Rater assumed parent (sleep disturbance scales); not stated. No significant effects of any intervention on sleep efficiency, sleep duration or daytime sleepiness. Effect on ADHD symptoms not reported in abstract.

evidence: intervention groups improved more than control groups in the five randomized controlled trials (-0.46, 95% CI = [-0.58, -0.35], k = 4)
notes: Abstract says five RCTs but k = 4. 'limited use of objective sleep measures'. 11 articles, 562 children in review.

topic: Sleep medication (incl. melatonin) for sleep in ADHD
notes: Abstract's category is 'sleeping pills'; it does not say how many of these are melatonin trials. Sleeping pills had no significant effect on overall sleep disturbance (-0.10, -0.41 to 0.22; k = 7). No ADHD-specific meta-analysis of melatonin was found; Parvataneni 2020 (PMID 32617211; 6 RCTs in ASD and/or ADHD) is a systematic review without a pooled estimate.

evidence: BLT significantly advanced the phase of DLMO by 31 min
notes: No meta-analysis found. Uncontrolled 2-week pilot in adults: dim-light melatonin onset advanced 31 min, mid-sleep 57 min; phase advance correlated with lower ADHD-RS total (p = 0.027). Sample size not in abstract.

evidence: reduction in ADHD symptoms (Standardized Mean Difference [SMD] = 0.68; 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.32, 1.04])
notes: Most proximal ratings (parents who received the training). Includes non-randomised but controlled trials. Conduct problems SMD 0.59 (0.29-0.90).

evidence: moderate effect sizes (ESs; Hedges' g) of 0.51 for ADHD symptoms, 0.4 for conduct problems, and 0.63 for negative parenting
notes: No CI in abstract. Parent-rated gains sustained at 3-12 month follow-up. Pair with independent-assessment row.

evidence: but no significant results on independently assessed ADHD symptoms
notes: Number not given in abstract, so es is null: independently assessed ADHD symptoms not significant (only negative parenting was). Groenman 2022 IPD meta-analysis (PMID 33932495): small-to-medium effects for raters most proximal to treatment; 'Blinded outcomes were available only for small preschool subsamples and limited measures'.

evidence: psychological interventions for parent (SMD = 0.42, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.51) and teacher rated symptoms (SMD = 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.38)
notes: Pre-post meta-meta-analysis of 16 meta-analyses. Medication for comparison: parent 0.67 (0.60-0.74), teacher 0.68 (0.54-0.82): medication effects are the same across raters, psychological effects are not.

evidence: psychological interventions for parent (SMD = 0.42, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.51) and teacher rated symptoms (SMD = 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.38)
notes: Teacher rating is 60% of the parent rating. No meta-analyses available for combined treatment.

evidence: effective in improving combined ADHD (d = -0.28, p < 0.0001), inattention (d = -0.33, p < 0.0001)
notes: No CI in abstract. Hyperactivity/impulsivity d = -0.09 (ns); academic performance d = 0.37; externalising d = -0.32. Authors flag high heterogeneity and 'potential reporter bias'. Search was limited to three journals. Gaastra 2016 (PMID 26886218): classroom interventions on off-task behaviour, within-subject designs MSMD 0.92, single-subject designs 3.08.

comparison: training vs no intervention or waiting list
journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
evidence: teacher-rated core ADHD symptoms at end of treatment for all eligible trials (SMD -0.26, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.05; 14 trials, 1379 participants; I2= 69%
notes: Cochrane. Authors call the finding 'questionable' (not robust in sensitivity analyses, high risk of bias). Teacher-rated social skills SMD 0.11 (0.00-0.22; 11 trials, I2 0%).

evidence: alternative/complement intervention (25 trials, 1195 participants) were less effective by the ES of -0.384 (P = .004) and -0.419 (P = .028), respectively
notes: Metric is an adjusted difference in effect size relative to psychostimulants (107 trials, n = 9883); negative = less effective than stimulants. Non-stimulant drugs -0.384. Parent behavioural therapy -0.308 (p = .095) and stimulant + PBT -0.196 (p = .209) did not differ significantly. Network meta-analysis Catala-Lopez 2017 (PMID 28700715; 190 trials, n = 26,114): behavioural therapy and stimulants superior to placebo; 'lack of evidence for cognitive training, neurofeedback, antidepressants, antipsychotics, dietary therapy, fatty acids'.

certainty: GRADE assessed; level not in abstract
evidence: moderate effects on global functioning at post-treatment (SMD = 0.47) that increased at follow-up (SMD = 0.67)
notes: 70 studies (5152 participants) of which 38 RCTs; abstract does not say which designs feed each estimate. No CI. Post-treatment 0.47. Quality-of-life effects smaller and not significant at follow-up. Follow-ups typically 3 months; reliance on self-report. Symptom improvement predicted QoL but not functioning.

certainty: CINeMA low or very low for most
evidence: long-term (SMD: -3.61, 95%CI: -4.66 to -2.56) core symptoms
notes: Implausibly large SMDs (short-term -4.43, -5.50 to -3.37), which suggests a scaling or unit problem; treat as a ranking only, not as an effect size. 48.6% of trials high risk of bias. k and n are network totals. CBT ranked first of 10 non-drug therapies.

evidence: No high certainty, long term evidence was found for any intervention
notes: BMJ umbrella review (47 meta-analytic reports, 221 re-estimated meta-analyses). Full text: only mindfulness in adults showed apparently large effects on self-reported symptoms at medium-term follow-up, very low certainty. Sibley 2025 (PMID 39370392, adolescents, 63 RCTs, no pooling): maintenance up to 3 years for cognitive/behavioural treatments, moderate quality because participants cannot be blinded.

evidence: DCDs were found to significantly increase daily step count (WMD=664.87, 95% CI: 463.22 to 866.51
notes: signal: urgency. Metric is weighted mean difference in steps/day, not standardized. Adults with cardiometabolic risk factors. k and n are for the whole review (29 RCTs), not the step-count pool. Weight loss WMD -1.90 kg (-2.59 to -1.21), I2 70%. GRADE was done but ratings are not in the abstract. Authors note no follow-up beyond 12 months.

comparison: evenly spaced imposed deadlines vs self-imposed/end deadlines
evidence: changes in the deadlines had a negligible effect on the three performance metrics
notes: signal: urgency. No meta-analysis of deadline effects was found. This is a replication of Study 2 of Ariely & Wertenbroch 2002 (PMID 12009041), the usual citation for 'imposed deadlines beat self-imposed ones'; it did not replicate. Europe PMC also lists a 2026 retraction notice for the original paper (PMID 42684323, title 'Retraction: Procrastination, Deadlines, and Performance: Self-Control by Precommitment'; no abstract text). No effect size in abstract. University students.

evidence: We found no difference between groups in invested mental effort or task completion.
notes: signal: urgency. No meta-analysis found for Pomodoro or timeboxing. Single student experiment: self-regulated breaks gave longer sessions with more fatigue and distraction and lower concentration and motivation, but no difference in task completion. A 2025 scoping review exists (PMID 41107936, seen by title only). No pooled estimate anywhere.

comparison: closer to goal vs further from goal
outcome: effort / purchase rate as reward approaches
evidence: participants in a real café reward program purchase coffee more frequently the closer they are to earning a free coffee
notes: signal: progress (also urgency). No meta-analysis of goal-gradient effects in humans found (Europe PMC: 0 hits with review filter). Landmark field studies, outside the 2015+ window; no standardized effect in abstract. Illusory progress (2 bonus stamps on a 12-stamp card) sped completion. Abstract read via Crossref API. Consumer reward programs, not task initiation.

evidence: When applying robust estimation methods, their overall effect size dropped from 0.36 to 0.15
notes: signal: none (planning cue; closest to urgency by fixing a when-then trigger). k = 642 independent tests. The paper's own abstract (read via OpenAlex API) gives only a range, '.27 <= d <= .66' across outcome types; larger with if-then format, high motivation and rehearsed plans. The 0.36 overall figure was read in Breitwieser 2026 full text (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13655945), which cites it. Not in PubMed; publisher page returned HTTP 403.

evidence: When applying robust estimation methods, their overall effect size dropped from 0.36 to 0.15
notes: signal: none (planning cue). Bias-corrected estimate (robust estimation) as quoted in Breitwieser 2026 full text (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13655945); not seen in the original paper. Effect falls by more than half after correction.

evidence: small-to-medium effect of implementation intentions in children (Hedge's g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.21; 0.41])
notes: signal: none (planning cue). Registered report. 52 effect sizes from 42 studies, mean age 10.67. Stronger in younger children and (in some analyses) children with ADHD. Full text: small-study effects, effect shrinks when outliers excluded, recent studies report smaller effects, z-curve suggests significant results over-represented.

evidence: averaging across those for children with ADHD or at higher likelihood of having ADHD ( g = 0.55)
notes: signal: none (planning cue). Subgroup figure from full text (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13655945); no CI or k seen. Full text: 'all included studies involving children with ADHD ... were conducted between 2004 and 2011', so this rests on a few small old studies with no recent replication. No adult ADHD pooled estimate found.

topic: Implementation intentions, people with mental health problems
evidence: forming implementation intentions had a large-sized effect on goal attainment (d+ = 0.99, k = 28, N = 1,636)
notes: signal: none (planning cue). Clinical and analogue samples; one very large outlier excluded. Small studies (mean n about 58). Breitwieser 2026 full text notes the eight child effect sizes in this review average d = 0.57. Much larger than general-population estimates: either small-study inflation or larger benefit where self-regulation is weak.

evidence: MCII to be effective for goal attainment with a small to medium effect size (g = 0.336)
notes: signal: meaning (contrast desired future with obstacle) plus planning. 24 independent effect sizes from 21 studies. Experimenter-delivered g = 0.465 vs document-delivered g = 0.277. Authors state 'because of some publication bias, the actual effect sizes may be smaller'.

evidence: main effect of mental contrasting on health outcomes, adjusted Hedges' g = 0.28 (SE = .07), 95% CI [0.13-0.43]
notes: signal: meaning. At up to three months (k = 5) g = 0.38 [0.20-0.55]. MCII (k = 7) g = 0.28 [0.14-0.42]: adding implementation intentions did not strengthen mental contrasting in this small subset.

journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
evidence: a small positive unique effect of goal setting across a range of behaviors, d = .34 (CI [.28, .41])
notes: signal: progress (with social presence when public). k = 141 papers, 384 effect sizes. Larger when the goal was difficult, set publicly, or a group goal; weaker evidence for external monitoring without feedback and face-to-face delivery.

evidence: teacher- and parent-rated outcome measures of organizational skills were g=0.54 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.91) and g=0.83
notes: signal: none (external structure and planning; closest to progress). Children and adolescents with ADHD. Rater effect: parent-rated (unblinded, involved in treatment) larger than teacher-rated. Teacher-rated inattention g = 0.26 (0.01 to 0.52); GPA g = 0.29 (0.07 to 0.51).

evidence: teacher- and parent-rated outcome measures of organizational skills were g=0.54 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.91) and g=0.83 (95% CI 0.32 to 1.34)
notes: signal: none (external structure and planning). Parent-rated inattention g = 0.56 (0.38 to 0.74) vs teacher-rated 0.26. Parents are the more proximal, unblinded rater.

comparison: gym-only access to audiobooks vs control
evidence: full and intermediate treatment participants visited the gym 51% and 29% more frequently, respectively, than control participants, but treatment effects declined over time
notes: signal: reward (immediate pleasure). No meta-analysis of temptation bundling exists (Europe PMC: 0 hits with review filter, 2 without). es is percent more gym visits initially, not standardized. Effect declined over time, particularly after Thanksgiving. 61% would pay for the device. Pre-2015 landmark.

comparison: audiobook plus bundling encouragement vs control
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
evidence: boosted their likelihood of a weekly workout by 10–14% and average weekly workouts by 10–12% during and up to seventeen weeks post-intervention
notes: signal: reward (immediate pleasure). Range, not a point estimate, so es is null. Relative to giving an audiobook alone, encouraging bundling had only 'a modest positive effect'. Much smaller than the 51% in the 2014 study (n far larger). Abstract read via OpenAlex API. Gym members.

topic: Financial incentives for physical activity (during incentive)
evidence: FI had a moderate effect during short-term interventions (standardized mean difference [SMD] [95 % CI] = 0.52 [0.25-0.78]
notes: signal: reward. n is for all 29 included studies; 15 in step-count meta-analyses. Median incentive $1.19 USD/day. Moderated by study length, incentive size, wearable use and goal setting. Pair with next row for post-withdrawal effect.

topic: Financial incentives for physical activity (after withdrawal)
outcome: daily step count at follow-up after incentive withdrawn
evidence: and a small effect in follow-up (SMD [95 % CI] = 0.20 [0.01-0.40], p = 0.04)
notes: signal: reward. Wear-off: effect falls from 0.52 to 0.20 once the incentive stops; only 3 of 8 studies reported positive follow-up effects. Lower CI bound touches zero.

evidence: very small pooled effect size for self-incentives (k = 7, N = 1,161), which was statistically significant, d+ = 0.17, CI [0.06, 0.29]
notes: signal: reward. Self-administered rewards are far weaker than externally delivered ones. No eligible studies of self-reward (reward after success) were found at all. Authors question why the technique is so widely used.

comparison: reward for attendance vs non-reward comparison
evidence: a moderate effect (d = 0.47, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.25, 0.69]) of ATT CM on attendance
notes: signal: reward. Substance-use treatment samples. More frequent rewards gave larger effects. Abstinence effect smaller, d = 0.22 [0.12, 0.33]. A separate review of contingency management in chronic health conditions (Ellis 2021, PMID 33302054, 20 RCTs) reports no pooled number in the abstract but states 'The effects of CM tend to dissipate when the contingency is removed'. No contingency-management meta-analysis in ADHD found.

comparison: incentive vs no or lower incentive
evidence: The corrected estimates are zero or tiny across contexts of field experiments
notes: signal: reward. Preprint; 1,568 estimates. No point estimate in abstract. After correcting for publication bias with Bayesian model averaging, field-experiment effects are zero or tiny; laboratory effects significant but weak. Shows large publication-bias inflation in the incentive-performance literature.

outcome: free-choice intrinsic motivation (persistence after reward removed)
evidence: engagement-contingent, completion-contingent, and performance-contingent rewards significantly undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = -0.40, -0.36, and -0.28, respectively)
notes: signal: reward (undermining effect). Pre-2015 landmark, still the reference. Negative es = harm. k = 128 is the whole review. Positive verbal feedback enhanced free-choice behaviour (d = 0.33) and interest (d = 0.31). Tangible rewards more detrimental for children than college students. Cerasoli 2014 (PMID 24491020, k = 183, N = 212,468) adds that incentives predict performance quantity and intrinsic motivation predicts quality (rho .21 to .45).

evidence: the largest effect for cognitive control RT (Cohen's d = 0.807), followed by memory accuracy (Cohen's d = 0.537)
notes: signal: reward. Laboratory reward-anticipation paradigms (monetary incentive delay style); 74 effect sizes from 56 publications. Trial-level laboratory contrasts, so not directly comparable with intervention SMDs. Effects 'highly sensitive to contextual parameters'. No ADHD subgroup reported in abstract.

evidence: and cognitive control accuracy (Cohen's d = 0.286)
notes: signal: reward. 70 effect sizes from 53 publications. Reward speeds responding much more (0.807) than it improves accuracy (0.286). Memory encoding accuracy d = 0.537 (43 publications, N = 2072).

topic: Reinforcement effects on inhibitory control in ADHD
comparison: reinforced vs non-reinforced task; ADHD vs controls
evidence: reinforcement can normalize inhibitory control in children and adolescents with ADHD to the baseline level of controls
notes: signal: reward. The only pooled evidence found on reward and task performance in ADHD. No numbers in the abstract (full text not open access), so es is null. Abstract adds that inhibitory control 'may improve to a larger extent in youth with ADHD compared with controls'. Children and adolescents only; no adult estimate; laboratory tasks.

evidence: small effects of gamification on cognitive ( g = .49, 95% CI [0.30, 0.69], k = 19, N = 1686)
notes: signal: reward, progress, novelty. Not in PubMed; abstract read via OpenAlex API. Design label is approximate: randomization was a tested moderator, so non-randomized studies are included. Cognitive effect stable in high-rigor subsplit; motivational and behavioural effects 'less stable'. Published online 2019, issue 2020.
signal: reward, progress, novelty. Effect 'less stable' when restricted to high-rigor studies. Period of time was tested as a moderator; the abstract does not report a wear-off.

evidence: and behavioral learning outcomes ( g = .25, 95% CI [0.04, 0.46], k = 9, N = 951)
notes: signal: reward, progress, novelty, social presence. Game fiction and combining competition with collaboration were significant moderators. Less stable in high-rigor subsplit.

evidence: an overall significant large effect size (g = 0.822 [0.567 to 1.078])
notes: signal: reward, progress, novelty. 'more than 5,071 participants'. Much larger than Sailer 2020 (0.25 to 0.49); includes theses and conference papers (full text Table 1); no bias-corrected estimate in abstract. Duration of gameful experience was a significant moderator (direction not stated in abstract).

topic: Gamification and physical activity (end of intervention)
evidence: small to medium summary effect of gamified interventions on PA behavior (Hedges g=0.42, 95% CI 0.14-0.69)
notes: signal: reward, progress, novelty. Versus inactive controls g = 0.58 (0.08-1.07). See next two rows for active-control and follow-up estimates.

topic: Gamification and physical activity (vs non-gamified active control)
evidence: active control groups that included a nongamified PA intervention (Hedges g=0.23, 95% CI 0.05-0.41)
notes: signal: reward, progress, novelty. The specific added value of game elements is about half the headline effect. Consistent with Nishi 2024 (gamified vs non-gamified apps).

topic: Gamification and physical activity (follow-up after intervention)
outcome: physical activity about 14 weeks after end
evidence: follow-up averaging 14 weeks after the end of the intervention) was weaker, with a very small to small effect (Hedges g=0.15, 95% CI 0.07-0.23)
notes: signal: reward, progress, novelty. Wear-off: 0.42 falls to 0.15 at follow-up. Authors read the persisting effect as 'not just a novelty effect'; the two-thirds drop is still the clearest pooled wear-off estimate found.

evidence: resulted in trivial increases in steps (489 steps/day [64 to 914]; high)
notes: signal: reward, progress. Metric is mean difference in steps/day. 36 trials, 49 comparisons, interventions of 8 weeks or longer. Authors call the step gain 'trivial' with high GRADE certainty. Body weight -0.70 kg (-1.18 to -0.22), moderate certainty.

evidence: a moderate effect (g = 0.44) of high curiosity states on the recall of task-specific information and a small effect (g = 0.13)
notes: signal: curiosity. 47 independent studies. Not moderated by age group, recall schedule, type of curiosity or exposure duration. Outcome is memory, not task initiation or sustained attention. ADHD not mentioned in abstract.

evidence: and a small effect (g = 0.13) on the recall of incidental information
notes: signal: curiosity. Spill-over of curiosity to unrelated material is small.

topic: Novelty effects on attention or task motivation
comparison: novel vs familiar task or stimulus
notes: signal: novelty. Europe PMC title search for novelty or curiosity with review filter gave 15 hits: neuroimaging syntheses, infant looking, genetics, and the curiosity-memory meta-analysis. No pooled estimate of novelty as an intervention for attention, engagement or task starting, in ADHD or the general population; an ADHD-specific search (interest/novelty in title) gave 0 hits. Gap. pub_year is the search year.

evidence: small-to-medium effect (N of standardized mean difference [SMD] = 44, mean SMD [M SMD] = 0.33, 95% CI [0.24, 0.42]
notes: signal: movement. k = 30 systematic reviews (383 unique studies). Attention 0.37, executive function 0.36, memory 0.23, information processing 0.20. Largest when tested after exercise (0.32). Age, cognitive status, intensity, type and duration did not moderate.

topic: Acute physical activity and cognition, young adults (bias-adjusted)
evidence: Acute exercise was found to have a small beneficial effect on cognition (g = 0.13 ± 0.04; BF = 3.67)
notes: signal: movement. Bayesian hierarchical model, 651 effect sizes, trim-and-fill applied. The ± 0.04 is as reported (type of interval not stated), so CI left null. Bayes factor 3.67 is only moderate evidence. Much smaller than the 0.33 from the meta-review of published meta-analyses. Ishihara 2021 IPD meta-analysis (PMID 34147558; no numbers in abstract) found larger benefit in those with lower pre-test performance.

topic: Single exercise session in ADHD, children
evidence: a single exercise session can improve executive function in children and adolescents with ADHD (g = 0.17, 95% CI [0.05, 0.29], P = 0.007)
notes: signal: movement. Three-level meta-analysis; GRADE low. Type, duration, intensity, age, control condition and design were not moderators. No publication bias detected.

topic: Acute exercise in ADHD, adults (inhibitory control)
comparison: single exercise bout vs non-exercise control
evidence: Acute exercise interventions exerted a moderate positive effect on inhibitory control (Hedges' g = 0.55, 95% CI [0.32, 0.79], p < 0.001)
notes: signal: movement. k = 8 is all studies in the meta-analysis, so the pool for this outcome may be smaller. Adult effect (0.55) is about three times the child estimate (0.17) but from very few studies. Chronic exercise in adults: mixed, not pooled.

topic: Acute exercise in ADHD, adults (core symptoms)
comparison: single exercise bout vs non-exercise control
evidence: a small beneficial effect on core symptoms (Hedges' g = 0.23, 95% CI [0.03, 0.43], p = 0.024)
notes: signal: movement. Rater assumed self-report (not stated in abstract). k is for the whole meta-analysis.

evidence: ADHD core symptoms (SMD = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.39 to 0.61) and executive functions (SMD = 0.77, 95% CI: 0.62 to 0.93)
notes: signal: movement. Included for contrast with the acute rows: programmes of repeated exercise pool at 0.77 vs 0.17 for one session. k = 45 meta-analyses (overlapping). Certainty low. Core symptoms SMD 0.50 (0.39 to 0.61). No effect on academic achievement. Belongs mainly to Area E.

evidence: Pooled estimates favored active breaks for attention (SMD =  - 0.53) and inhibitory control (SMD =  - 0.49)
notes: signal: movement. Negative sign favours active breaks as reported. k = 25 RCTs in the review. No CI in abstract; 'substantial heterogeneity'. Exploratory: 5 to 15 minute, acute, single-session formats looked larger. General school pupils, not ADHD.

topic: Interrupting sitting with standing or activity breaks (executive function)
journal: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
evidence: improvements in executive function (k = 16 studies; Hedges' g = 0.18; 95% CI: 0.03 to 0.32; p = 0.016)
notes: signal: movement. Randomized crossover trials; n = 433 across all 21 trials. Memory g = 0.37 (0.13 to 0.61). Larger in older adults and people with overweight; walking breaks most consistent. Closest pooled evidence for standing/walking desks; an active-workstation review (Dupont 2019, PMID 30692162) is narrative only and notes treadmill desks reduce typing and mouse performance.

topic: Interrupting sitting with standing or activity breaks (attention)
journal: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
evidence: or attention (k = 5 studies; Hedges' g = - 0.08; 95% CI: -0.38 to 0.22; p = 0.575)
notes: signal: movement. Null for attention, in contrast to the child classroom active-break result (-0.53 favouring breaks). Low certainty.

topic: White or pink noise in ADHD
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: a small but statistically significant benefit of white and pink noise on task performance (g = 0.249, 95% CI [0.135, 0.363], p < .0001)
notes: signal: none of the nine (external stimulation/arousal). Children and college-age young adults with ADHD or elevated symptoms. Minimal heterogeneity, no publication bias found. No brown-noise studies exist. GRADE was applied; rating not in abstract. Laboratory tasks only.

topic: White or pink noise in people without ADHD
journal: Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry
evidence: In non-ADHD comparison groups (k = 11, N = 335), white and pink noise had a negative effect (g = -0.212, 95% CI [-0.355, -0.069]
notes: signal: none of the nine (external stimulation/arousal). Sign reversal by population: the same manipulation helps ADHD (+0.249) and harms non-ADHD (-0.212). Clearest pooled example of an individual-difference moderator in this area. The abstract gives N = 335 for both groups.

evidence: Based on 31 effect sizes, the results indicated an overall medium and significant effect size (g = 0.40)
notes: signal: none of the nine (auditory stimulation). 15 studies, 31 effect sizes; no CI or bias-corrected estimate in abstract; the accompanying systematic review 'reveal[s] conflicting results'. No ADHD-specific pooled estimate.

evidence: a small and positive mean effect size ( d = 0.314) in favor of the BM condition
notes: signal: reward (pleasure) / none of the nine. 71 effect sizes from 47 experimental and quasi-experimental studies including dissertations and conference papers. Medium effect when music was played before the assessment. Abstract read via Crossref API. A 2025 ADHD music-therapy meta-analysis (PMID 40680190) reports an internally inconsistent estimate ('effect size: 1.18; CI: -3.8 - 0.21', I2 = 92%) and was not extracted.

evidence: Stroop performance in both social and non-social contexts (g = 0.30, [0.17; 0.44], p < .001)
notes: signal: social presence. Number from full text (https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12717298); abstract gives no number. Stronger with an attentive than an inattentive audience and null with an evaluative audience; effect shrinks with more trials (beta = -0.002). Not evident for correct responses. Laboratory task; ADHD not examined as far as seen.

evidence: the presence of others had small effects, accounting for .3% to 3% of the variance in the typical experiment
notes: signal: social presence. Pre-2015 landmark; no newer general meta-analysis of mere presence on cognitive task performance was found. Presence speeds simple tasks and slows and impairs complex ones; facilitation of simple-task accuracy 'vulnerable to the file drawer problem'. n is 'nearly 24,000'. Abstract read via OpenAlex API.

comparison: human or AI body double vs working alone
evidence: Results from 12 participants show they finished tasks faster and perceived greater accuracy and sustained attention in C2 and C3 compared to C1
notes: signal: social presence. No meta-analysis and no randomized trial of body doubling in ADHD found (Europe PMC: 1 hit for body doubling / virtual co-working, a non-ADHD preprint). This is a 12-person virtual-reality bricklaying study, not peer reviewed; no effect size. The abstract itself says 'prior work found no conclusive effectiveness and noted NDs' discomfort with social presence'. Abstract read via arXiv API. Gap.

comparison: virtual co-working app vs working alone
evidence: the adjusted mean difference was −9.5 (95% confidence interval (CI) −13.4 to −5.5)
notes: signal: social presence. Open-label randomized crossover trial, 30-minute task periods, existing users of the app (self-selected), self-rated outcomes only; 'objective performance, productivity ... require further study'. Not ADHD. Preprint. Adjusted mean difference on the NASA-TLX score.

topic: Human guidance / accountability in digital interventions
evidence: guidance significantly increases the average amount of intervention completion [g = 0.29, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.18-0.40]
notes: signal: social presence (accountability). Web-based mental health interventions. Proportion completing: log OR = 0.50 (0.34-0.66); full completion rates 12% higher with guidance. Closest pooled evidence for accountability partners; no meta-analysis of accountability partners as such.

topic: Peer/social support features in digital interventions (vs any control)
comparison: intervention with social support vs control
evidence: moderate effect sizes of Hedges' g=-0.34 (95% CI -0.47 to -0.21, p<0.001) in comparison to different control conditions
notes: signal: social presence. Negative favours intervention. 96% implemented social support as 'social facilitation' (seeing others use the intervention, e.g. forum). This compares whole interventions with controls, so it does not isolate the social element; see next row.

topic: Peer/social support features in digital interventions (component studies)
comparison: same intervention with vs without social support
evidence: not significantly more effective in comparison to the same IMI without social support (Hedges' g=-0.08 (95% CI -0.22 to 0.05, p=0.19, I2=0%)
notes: signal: social presence. Dismantling design: the isolated effect of the social feature is near zero on symptoms, though 7 of 11 component studies reported higher adherence with social support. Shows the gap between package effect (-0.34) and component effect (-0.08).

evidence: providing choice enhanced intrinsic motivation, effort, task performance, and perceived competence
notes: signal: autonomy. Pre-2015 landmark; no newer general meta-analysis of choice found. Abstract gives no effect size, so es is null. Stronger for instructionally irrelevant choices, 2 to 4 successive choices, when no reward followed, and for children vs adults.

evidence: The true effects are instead small, uncertain, and potentially null.
notes: signal: autonomy. Robust Bayesian reanalysis of two meta-analyses (self-controlled practice, enhanced expectancies). Reporting bias 'substantially exaggerated' benefits; estimated average power of the original studies 6% (95% CI 5% to 13%). No point estimate in abstract. Motor-learning domain, but the best bias-corrected test of a pure choice manipulation.

journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
evidence: The sample-weighted average effect size for SDT interventions was d+ = .23
notes: signal: autonomy. Publication bias and small-sample bias present; effects 'remained significantly different from zero, albeit of smaller magnitude, after correction for bias (d+ >= .15)'. Autonomous motivation and perceived competence mediated effects. k and N not recorded (methods section of abstract not reviewed).

evidence: perceived autonomy support g = 0.84, autonomy g = 0.81, competence g = 0.63, relatedness g = 0.28, and motivation g = 0.41
notes: signal: autonomy. 74 studies, 80% RCTs. Self-rated proximal mediators move a lot (perceived autonomy support 0.84) while behaviour moves little (Sheeran 2020: d = 0.23, 0.15 corrected). Individual techniques had limited independent impact; combinations matter.

evidence: and promoted goal attainment (d+ = 0.40, 95% CI [0.32, 0.48])
notes: signal: progress (social presence when public). Interventions raised monitoring frequency by d = 1.98 [1.71, 2.24]. Larger when progress was reported or made public and when physically recorded.

comparison: feedback vs no or less feedback
evidence: indicate a medium effect (d = 0.48) of feedback on student learning
notes: signal: progress. 435 studies, 994 effect sizes, N > 61,000; Europe PMC lists publication year 2019. Significant heterogeneity; feedback has higher impact on cognitive and motor outcomes than on motivational and behavioural outcomes, so the estimate may overstate the effect on getting started.

evidence: competence beliefs (g = 0.36), mindset (g = 0.27), and utility value (g = 0.19), while smaller for interest (g = 0.11)
notes: signal: meaning. Preprint; 289 effect sizes from 38 RCTs; overall g = 0.20. By intervention type: personal values 0.33, task value 0.18, framing 0.18. Interest moved least (0.11). Not moderated by publication year, peer review status or study quality. Outcomes are self-reported motivation, not behaviour.

evidence: an average mean effect size of d = 0.49 (95% confidence interval = [0.43, 0.56])
notes: signal: meaning (also autonomy). 92 independent effect sizes from 74 papers; includes quasi-experiments, and 'randomized designs having smaller effect sizes than quasi-experimental designs'. Ten years later an RCT-only preprint (Boyle 2026) finds g = 0.20: a decline with rigor and year. Abstract read via Crossref API.

evidence: low magnitude (dIG+ = 0.41, z = 16.01, p < 0.00), with a 95% confidence interval whose values tended to lie between 0.36 and 0.45
notes: signal: meaning. 144 experimental studies, high school and university students. No bias correction reported in abstract. A separate meta-analysis of well-being outcomes (Zhang 2025, PMID 41143765, 129 tests) reports ES = 0.29 for general well-being. Identity-threat buffering, not task starting.

evidence: Overall effect size g when comparing treatment to control was 0.34, 95% Confidence Interval [0.11, 0.56]
notes: signal: none (multi-component). 12 RCTs, 21 comparisons. Self-report outcome only, unblinded, inactive comparators. Egger test not significant. No newer RCT meta-analysis found; no ADHD-specific trial pooled.

evidence: using cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) found an effect size g of 0.55, 95% CI [0.32, 0.77]
notes: signal: none (multi-component). Subgroup of 'three out of four' CBT studies, N = 236. Self-report, inactive control.

evidence: We present a meta-analysis of 24 studies on procrastination interventions (total k = 44, N = 1173).
notes: signal: none (multi-component). Abstract read on the University of Amsterdam repository page (https://dare.uva.nl/id/12627c11-4b2f-401a-b9fc-1a7ee4d7cf91): 'A large reduction in procrastination after the interventions was found'; CBT strongest; duration not a moderator; stable at follow-up. No numeric effect seen, so es is null. Population not stated in abstract.

evidence: Across studies, ADHD symptoms were consistently positively associated with procrastination. Inattention emerged as the most robust correlate.
notes: signal: none. Systematic review without pooling; mostly cross-sectional. No meta-analysis of the ADHD-procrastination association and no trial of a procrastination intervention in ADHD was found. Gap.

evidence: significant improvements in habit scores pre- to post-intervention across different habits (standardised mean difference: 0.69, 95% CI: 0.49-0.88)
notes: signal: none (repetition/cue). Pre-post, uncontrolled; 11 of 20 studies high risk of bias. Time to automaticity: medians 59 to 66 days, means 106 to 154 days, individual range 4 to 335 days (large individual variability). Self-selected habits and morning practice were stronger (autonomy, timing).

journal: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity
evidence: habit formation interventions significantly increased PA habit (SMD = 0.31, 95% CI 0.14-0.48, P < .001)
notes: signal: none (repetition/cue). Controlled estimate is under half the pre-post estimate (0.69). Follow-up of 12 weeks or less gave larger effects than longer follow-up (wear-off). Meta-regression: problem solving beta = 0.36 (0.17-0.55); social reward linked to lower effectiveness (beta = -0.40).

evidence: JITAIs/EMIs showed a small between-group effect (g=0.15, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.26, p=0.003)
notes: signal: none (timely prompt; closest to urgency). Follow-up effects at 1 and 3-6 months in nine studies. Risk of bias moderate to high for adherence and missing data. k and n not recorded (methods section of abstract not reviewed).

evidence: (2) non-JITAI treatments (k = 21), g = 0.89
notes: signal: none (timely prompt). 33 early studies; vs waitlist (k = 9) g = 1.65. Decline effect: 0.89 to 1.65 in 2020 against 0.15 in the 2025 meta-analysis. A 2023 pre-post synthesis (Xu, PMID 37521518, 592 participants) gives g = 0.77 (0.32 to 1.22). No ADHD JITAI meta-analysis found.

topic: Prompts and reminders for engagement with digital interventions
evidence: compared to no strategy for dichotomous outcomes (relative risk [RR] 1.27, 95% CI 1.01-1.60, I(2)=71%)
notes: signal: none (cue; closest to urgency). 14 studies with 8,774 participants, 9 in meta-analyses. Authors call the effect 'borderline positive'. One small study: prompts announcing new content, and prompts sent soon after starting, engaged more (novelty, timing).

evidence: The pooled odds ratio of the randomized control trials was 1.62 (1.35-1.94)
notes: signal: none (cue; closest to urgency). 13 RCTs of 28 studies. No difference by timing, frequency or content of reminder. Health-care attendance, a one-off dated action, not self-initiated task starting.

journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
evidence: small to medium effect size of Cohen's d = 0.45 (95% CI [0.39, 0.52])
notes: signal: none (environment design). 'more than 200 studies', over 450 effect sizes. Decision structure outperforms decision information and decision assistance. Authors report 'moderate publication bias'. Szaszi 2022 and Maier 2022 quote d = 0.43 (corrected dataset; a correction notice exists, PMID 35507882). See next row.

journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
notes: signal: none (environment design). Robust Bayesian meta-analysis of the Mertens data (Table 1, https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC9351501): random effects 0.43 falls to 0.04 (95% credible interval), or 0.11 [0.00, 0.24] using most precise estimates. 'Assistance' category: 0.22 falls to 0.01 [0.00, 0.07]; information 0.25 to 0.00; structure 0.58 to 0.12 [0.00, 0.43]. Evidence for heterogeneity remains, 'which implies that some nudges might be effective'.

evidence: In the Academic Journals papers, the average impact of a nudge is very large—an 8.7 percentage point take‐up effect, which is a 33.4% increase
notes: signal: none (environment design). Metric is percentage-point difference in take-up. Compare next row. Abstract read via Crossref API.

topic: Nudges run at scale by two Nudge Units (percentage points)
evidence: In the Nudge Units sample, the average impact is still sizable and highly statistically significant, but smaller at 1.4 percentage points, an 8.0% increase
notes: signal: none (environment design). 126 RCTs covering 23 million people, including all trials run by two US Nudge Units. One sixth of the journal estimate; 'selective publication ... exacerbated by low statistical power, explains about 70 percent of the difference'.

evidence: 45% of these interventions significantly increased weekly gym visits by 9% to 27%; the top-performing intervention offered microrewards
notes: signal: reward (top performer: microrewards for returning after a missed workout). 54 four-week digital programmes in one population. 'Only 8% of interventions induced behaviour change that was significant and measurable after the four-week intervention' (wear-off). Forecasts by impartial judges 'failed to predict which interventions would be most effective'. A 2-million-person savings megastudy (PMID 41030290) found reminder emails raised one-time deposits by 0.05 percentage points.

evidence: Significant effects in favor of caffeine were found for both accuracy, g = 0.27, and reaction time, g = 0.28
notes: signal: none of the nine (pharmacological arousal). Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in rested healthy adults. Doses of 200 mg or more worked better; accuracy shows a quadratic dose-response. Not related to habitual consumption. Same size as white noise in ADHD (0.249).

evidence: Significant effects in favor of caffeine were found for both accuracy, g = 0.27, and reaction time, g = 0.28
notes: signal: none of the nine (pharmacological arousal). Positive linear dose-response for reaction time. Blinded, placebo-controlled: one of the few blinded estimates in this area.

signal: none. Europe PMC search for 'dopamine fasting' or 'dopamine detox' in title or abstract (with digital detox and social media abstinence in title) and review filter returned 1 hit, a social media abstinence meta-analysis (next row). No pooled evidence and no trial identified for dopamine fasting. Gap. pub_year is the search year.

topic: Social media abstinence (nearest proxy for 'detox' claims)
outcome: positive affect, negative affect, life satisfaction
evidence: The analyses revealed no significant effects of social media abstinence interventions on positive affect, negative affect, or life satisfaction.
notes: signal: none. Preregistered; 10 studies, 38 effect sizes. No numeric estimates in abstract. Duration of abstinence unrelated to outcomes. Outcomes are well-being, not attention or task starting.

topic: Habituation, wear-off and rotation of engagement strategies
comparison: rotating vs fixed strategy; early vs late effect
notes: signal: novelty. No meta-analysis or trial of rotating strategies found (Europe PMC: 0 hits for ADHD strategy rotation/habituation; 16 hits for novelty effect or sustained engagement in digital interventions, none pooling a time course). Wear-off is visible only indirectly in other rows: gamification 0.42 to 0.15 at follow-up; incentives 0.52 to 0.20 after withdrawal; temptation bundling 'declined over time'; megastudy 8% of programmes with lasting effect; habit effects smaller beyond 12 weeks. Gap. pub_year is the search year.

topic: Individual differences in which strategy works (heterogeneity, n-of-1)
notes: signal: none. No meta-analysis of n-of-1 trials or of treatment-effect heterogeneity for engagement strategies was found. Nearest: Punja 2016 (PMID 27060386) pooled N-of-1 trials of stimulants in paediatric ADHD with RCTs (method paper, no behavioural strategies); Bryan 2021 (PMID 34294901) and Szaszi 2022 (PMID 35858388) argue narratively that effects are heterogeneous; Maier 2022 finds residual heterogeneity after bias correction. The only pooled person-by-treatment reversal is white/pink noise (ADHD +0.249 vs non-ADHD -0.212). Gap. pub_year is the search year.

outcome: Depression detection (AI on wearable data vs reference standard)
certainty: GRADE assessed; rating not stated in abstract
evidence: diagnostic odds ratio of 110.47 (95% CI 33.33-366.17) and AUC of 0.96 (95% CI 0.94-0.98)
notes: 16 studies (32 datasets), 1189 patients, 13,593 samples. Pooled sensitivity 0.89 (0.83-0.93), specificity 0.93 (0.87-0.96). Only 'moderate utility' for predicting episodes. Authors flag heterogeneity, reliance on retrospective and public datasets, non-standard methods; PROBAST+AI used. Earlier review (Abd-Alrazaq 2023, PMID 37147384, 54 studies) pooled best-model accuracy 0.89 but worst-model accuracy 0.70, i.e. reported accuracy depends heavily on which model per study is counted.

topic: Passive GPS mobility and depressive symptoms
outcome: Depressive symptoms vs GPS distance travelled
evidence: distance (r=-0.25, 95% CI -0.29 to -0.21), normalized entropy (r-0.17, 95% CI -0.29 to -0.04)
notes: Largest feature-level correlation; others smaller: location variance -0.17, entropy -0.13, clusters -0.11, homestay +0.10. 79% (15/19) of studies underpowered to detect r=.20; evidence of publication bias; within-person correlations (k=3) too heterogeneous to pool. Contrast with AUC 0.96 claimed by wearable-AI classifiers: the raw sensor-symptom signal is small.

topic: Wearable (Fitbit) ML screening for ADHD, children
evidence: ML models showed reasonable predictive performance for ADHD (AUC, 0.798; sensitivity, 0.756; specificity, 0.716; PPV, 0.159; and NPV, 0.976)
notes: No meta-analysis of passive sensing for ADHD diagnosis was found; this is the largest single study (79 with ADHD problems vs 1011 controls). PPV only 0.159 at this base rate. Other single studies: smartphone CPT plus phone sensors, 952 controls and 292 unmedicated ADHD, sensitivity 0.808, PR-AUC 0.799 (Casals 2025, PMID 41280456); De Crescenzo 2016 actigraphy meta-analysis (PMID 26163053, 24 studies, 2179 children) gives no pooled number in its abstract.

topic: MRI-based machine learning diagnosis of ADHD
evidence: SROC curve showed that AUC was 0.81 (95 % CI 0.77-0.84)
notes: Pooled sensitivity 0.74 (0.65-0.81), specificity 0.75 (0.67-0.81); 43 studies reviewed, 27 pooled. Deeks test used for publication bias; result not in abstract.

topic: EEG/MRI machine learning classification of ADHD (236 studies)
evidence: Overall reported classification accuracy across studies was high (87%), with a substantial upward trend over publication years
notes: Preprint (PsyArXiv); descriptive average, not a bivariate pooled estimate. Key moderators: smaller studies report higher accuracy than larger ones; accuracy rises with publication year; EEG, in-task recording and younger samples higher; very few studies use clinical comparison groups; many use validation prone to overfitting. Compare with pooled AUC 0.81 for MRI-only (Tian 2024).

topic: Risk of bias (PROBAST) in neuroimaging AI models for psychiatric diagnosis
outcome: Share of models at high overall risk of bias, %
evidence: 461 (83.1%; 95% CI, 80.0%-86.2%) were rated as having a high overall ROB based on the PROBAST
notes: 517 studies, 555 models. Inadequate sample size in 71.7% (68.0-75.6); 100% lacked calibration assessment; 99.1% did not handle data complexity; none judged applicable to clinical practice. k is studies; denominator is 555 models.

topic: Clinical prediction models in psychiatry: bias and external validation
outcome: Share of developed models at high risk of bias (PROBAST), %
evidence: 94.5% of developed prediction models were deemed to be at high risk of bias, largely due to inadequate or inappropriate analytic decisions
notes: 228 studies, 308 models (onset, course, treatment response). Only one-fifth of models externally validated; just one model had clinical utility formally assessed. Salazar de Pablo 2021 (PMID 32914178): of 584 prediction studies, 4.6% externally validated models and 0.2% considered for implementation.

topic: Sample size and ML accuracy: depression neuroimaging classification
outcome: MDD vs controls accuracy in full sample, %
journal: Neuropsychopharmacology : official publication of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology
evidence: trained and tested a classification model on the full dataset which yielded an accuracy of 61%
notes: Demonstration of small-sample inflation: resampling the same data gives accuracies up to 95% at N=20 and up to 75% at N=100, versus 61% at N=1868. Large test sets, not large training sets, protect against misestimation. Direct evidence that accuracy falls as sample size rises.

topic: Virtual-reality classroom CPT, ADHD vs controls
outcome: Omission, commission errors, hit reaction time
evidence: Results suggest that the virtual classroom CPTs reliably differentiate attention performance in persons with ADHD
notes: Pooled g values are in the paywalled full text and were not seen this session, so es is null. Abstract states results were 'generally consistent' with meta-analyses of 2D computerized CPTs, with 'subtle' differences; moderator analysis not possible. Gilboa 2021 (PMID 30371134): 13 studies, 9 pooled, N=431, significant group differences, numbers not in abstract. No pooled sensitivity/specificity for VR CPT found.

topic: VR-based executive-function assessment vs traditional tests
outcome: Correlation of VR assessment with traditional neuropsychological tests (Fisher z)
evidence: the pooled Fisher's z value was 0.454 (95% CI: 0.285-0.623; I 2 = 75.05
notes: Metric is Fisher z (about r=0.43). Full text: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11595626/fullTextXML . Funnel plot and Egger test showed significant publication bias (p<0.05). Not moderated by VR properties, clinical status or age. Moderate overlap means VR tasks are not interchangeable with standard tests.

topic: Wearable EEG sleep devices vs polysomnography
outcome: Five-stage sleep staging agreement (Cohen kappa, mean across studies)
evidence: the studies showed an overall ACC of 0.78 ± 0.07 and an overall κ of 0.68 ± 0.10, suggesting substantial agreement
notes: Mean ± SD across studies, not an inverse-variance pooled estimate. Full text: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC13055050/fullTextXML . Stage N1 kappa only 0.31 ± 0.15; wake 0.75 ± 0.12. Manual scoring beat automatic scoring for N1; more electrodes improved N3. This is the only pooled validity evidence found for consumer/wearable EEG and it concerns sleep, not waking attention markers.

topic: Consumer-grade EEG vs research-grade EEG for waking/attention measures
evidence: We identified 916 studies that used data recorded with consumer-grade EEG: 531 were reported in journal articles and 385 in conference papers
notes: Gap. Scoping review charted 916 consumer-EEG studies (Emotiv most used, then NeuroSky, OpenBCI, Muse) but validation was a minority use and no pooled validity estimate exists for waking EEG (theta/beta, ERPs) against research-grade systems. Single-device validations only (e.g. Krigolson 2017 Muse, PMID 28344546).

outcome: Overall diagnostic accuracy of generative AI models, %
evidence: Analysis of 83 studies revealed an overall diagnostic accuracy of 52.1%
notes: CI (47.0-57.1%) from full text https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11929846/fullTextXML . No significant difference vs physicians overall (p=0.10) or non-experts (p=0.93). PROBAST: 63/83 (76%) studies high risk of bias. Studies to June 2024.

topic: Generative AI vs expert physicians, diagnosis
outcome: Difference in diagnostic accuracy, percentage points (experts minus AI)
evidence: generative AI models overall were significantly inferior to expert physicians (difference in accuracy: 15.8% [95% CI: 4.4-27.1%], p = 0.007
notes: Positive value means experts more accurate than AI. Versus non-experts the difference was 0.6% (-14.5 to 15.7). Abstract gives only p=0.007. Several newer models (GPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro and others) were not significantly different from experts, so the gap is model- and date-dependent. Full text: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11929846/fullTextXML

topic: Physician plus LLM vs physician alone, diagnostic accuracy
evidence: LLM assistance was associated with a small improvement in diagnostic accuracy (Hedges’ g = 0.22, 95% CI [0.18, 0.27]
notes: Preprint (medRxiv); includes randomized and non-randomized comparative designs, so the design label is approximate. Effect varied substantially by LLM and medical field. Peer-reviewed counterpart (Wang 2026, NPJ Digit Med, PMID 41606089, 10 studies): diagnostic accuracy RR 1.59 (0.08-32.74, k=2, ns); composite score +4.88 points (0.65-9.12, k=2) with prediction interval -31.65 to 41.42; factual error rates about 26-36%; human+AI did not universally beat AI alone. Goh 2025 RCT (PMID 39910272, n=92): +6.5% (2.7-10.2) on management reasoning, and physician+GPT-4 no better than GPT-4 alone (-0.9%, -9.0 to 7.2).

topic: LLM-assisted lay users vs LLM alone (medical scenarios)
outcome: Correct identification of relevant condition by participants using an LLM, %
evidence: participants using the same LLMs identified relevant conditions in fewer than 34.5% of cases and disposition in fewer than 44.2%
notes: Preregistered randomized study. The same LLMs tested alone identified conditions in 94.9% of cases (disposition 56.3%); with real users performance was no better than control. Benchmarks and simulated patient interactions did not predict the failure. Value is an upper bound ('fewer than'). Key caution for simulating users with LLMs.

topic: Human-AI combinations vs best of human or AI alone
evidence: human-AI combinations performed significantly worse than the best of humans or AI alone (Hedges' g = -0.23; 95% confidence interval, -0.39 to -0.07)
notes: 106 experiments, 370 effect sizes, 2020 to mid-2023, preregistered. Decision tasks g=-0.27 (-0.44 to -0.10); content-creation tasks g=+0.19 (-0.09 to 0.48) (full text https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11659167/fullTextXML). Gains when humans outperform AI alone, losses when AI outperforms humans. Possible publication bias. Not health-specific.

topic: LLM chatbot vs health professionals: rated empathy
evidence: showed a standardized mean difference of 0.87 (95% CI, 0.54-1.20) favouring AI
notes: 15 studies 2023-2024, 13 pooled, all ChatGPT-3.5/4. Text-only replies judged by proxy raters, not by the patients concerned; non-verbal cues not assessed; ROBINS-I used. Two dermatology studies favoured humans.

outcome: Negative mental health symptoms (depression, anxiety, other)
evidence: The meta-analysis of 14 RCTs showed a statistically significant effect (effect size [ES]=0.30, P=.047, N=6314, 95% CI 0.004, 0.59
notes: 95% prediction interval -0.85 to 1.67, so a new trial could show harm or large benefit. Mostly non-WEIRD settings; social-oriented bots outperformed task-oriented. Protocol registered retrospectively. Du 2025 (PMID 41343858): LLM-based chatbots depression g=0.407 (-0.734 to 1.550), anxiety g=0.711 (-0.334 to 1.760), both non-significant; rule-based depression g=0.266 (0.020-0.512). Single RCT of a fine-tuned generative chatbot (Heinz 2025, NEJM AI, PMID 42932588) reported d=0.845-0.903 for depression symptoms.

evidence: Chatbots produced statistically significant reductions in depressive (g = 0.31, 95% CI [0.17, 0.46]) and anxiety symptoms (g = 0.28, 95% CI [0.05, 0.51])
notes: Anxiety g=0.28 (0.05-0.51), k=34, n=7621. Larger in clinical/subclinical than non-clinical samples (p=0.001). Full text: 35 of 39 trials high overall risk of bias, mainly outcome measurement; Egger test significant for depression (p=0.002). Earlier meta-analysis (He 2023, PMID 37115595, 32 RCTs, n=6089): depression g=0.29 (0.20-0.38), long-term effects mostly not significant.

topic: Commercial AI mental health chatbots, depression
evidence: Depression improved versus controls (18 RCTs; N = 3,170): g = -0.35 (95% CI: -0.56, -0.13), about 1.6 PHQ-9 points
notes: About 1.6 PHQ-9 points, below the 5-point minimal clinically important difference. Anxiety g=-0.37 (-0.87 to 0.12), net harm not excluded; loneliness g=-0.21 (-0.39 to -0.03). Completion 79.5% (68.0-87.6) with a 'scalability gradient'; attrition vs control RR 1.01 (0.79-1.29). Harms reporting uninterpretable: only 3 of 22 RCTs actively ascertained harms.

evidence: The meta-analytic overall attrition rate in the intervention group was 21.84% (95% CI 16.74%-27.36%; I2=94%)
notes: Trials of 8 weeks or less 18.05%; longer than 8 weeks 26.59%. Intervention arms lost more participants than controls. Higher attrition for stand-alone agents without human support, no symptom tracker, no visual representation, waitlist comparison.

topic: Mental health smartphone apps, depression (176 RCTs)
journal: World psychiatry : official journal of the World Psychiatric Association (WPA)
evidence: small effects on symptoms of depression (N=33,567, g=0.28, p<0.001; number needed to treat, NNT=11.5)
notes: Generalized anxiety g=0.26 (N=22,394, NNT 12.4). Robust to removing small and high-risk-of-bias trials. Less outcome variability in app than control arms (ratio of variance -0.14, -0.24 to -0.05). Larger with CBT features or chatbot technology. k=176 is all included RCTs. CI not given in abstract.

topic: Depression and anxiety app trials: attrition and adherence
evidence: The meta-analytic posttest attrition rate was 18.6% (95% PI, 2.4%-68.3%), and at follow-up, it was 28.4% (95% PI, 3.0%-83.7%)
notes: Source reports 95% prediction intervals, not CIs: post-test 2.4-68.3%, follow-up 28.4% (3.0-83.7). Uptake 92.4% (PI 48.4-99.4, 56 conditions); adherence 61.8% (PI 53.2-69.7, 21 conditions). Lower attrition with reminders, human contact, and no gamification. Attrition higher than waitlist (RR 1.49). Older estimate (Linardon 2020, PMID 31697093): 24.1% short-term, 35.5% longer-term.

evidence: significant decrease in overall ADHD symptoms (SMD = -0.33; 95 % CI = [-0.51, -0.16]) compared to the control groups
notes: Rater mix not stated in abstract; treated as mostly unblinded. Inattention -0.31 (-0.46 to -0.15); hyperactivity/impulsivity -0.15 (-0.29 to -0.02). Mei 2026 network meta-analysis (PMID 42358407, 37 RCTs, n=2922): inattention -0.44 (-0.62 to -0.26). Hao 2026 (PMID 42614105): 40.6% of 32 RCTs at high risk of bias. Umbrella review (Gabarron 2025, PMID 40264083, 26 reviews): evidence low quality, adverse effects reported in only 8 of 26 reviews; no pooled adherence or attrition rate exists for ADHD digital interventions.

topic: Computerized cognitive training for ADHD, probably blinded raters
evidence: showed no effect on ADHD total (SMD = 0.12, 95%CI[-0.01 to -0.25]) or hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms
notes: Abstract prints the upper bound as '-0.25' (apparent typo for 0.25). 36 RCTs, 14 with probably blinded outcome. Inattention 0.17 (0.02-0.31), rising to 0.40 (0.09-0.71, n=5) when assessed in the intervention delivery setting: a setting-specific effect. Working memory improved (verbal 0.38, visual-spatial 0.49) without transfer to other neuropsychological or academic outcomes. Compare with about -0.33 for digital interventions when raters are not restricted to blinded.

topic: Game-based digital therapeutics for ADHD, parent-rated
evidence: Game-based DTx improved inattention more than the control upon assessment by assessors (standard mean difference (SMD) 0.28, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.14-0.41; SMD 0.21
notes: Abstract lists the two assessor estimates 'respectively'; taken as parent 0.28 then teacher 0.21 (0.03-0.39). Medication beat game-based DTx on teacher-rated inattention (SMD -0.62, -1.04 to -0.20; indirect comparison). Hyperactivity/impulsivity 0.28 and 0.30.

topic: Computerized cognitive training for adults with ADHD
evidence: CCT compared to controls (k = 9, Hedge's g = 0.235, 95% CI [0.002, 0.467], p = 0.048
notes: Neither symptom severity nor specific cognitive outcomes (executive function, speed, working memory) improved significantly. Adults: effect confined to a composite cognitive score, borderline significance.

topic: Just-in-time adaptive and ecological momentary interventions, mental health
evidence: JITAIs/EMIs showed a small between-group effect (g=0.15, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.26, p=0.003)
notes: k, n and I2 from full text (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC12481328/fullTextXML): 23 studies, 2563 participants, I2=20%. Interventions shorter than 6 weeks showed greater longevity of effects (g=0.71, 0.18-1.24). Risk of bias moderate to high for adherence and missing data; authors call for a clearer definition of JITAI and decision rules. Sleep-focused meta-analysis (Xi 2026, PMID 42994167, 11 RCTs): insomnia severity SMD -0.87 (-1.32 to -0.42), depressive symptoms -0.76 (-1.23 to -0.29).

evidence: (1) waitlist-control conditions (k = 9), Hedges's g = 1.65 and (2) non-JITAI treatments (k = 21), g = 0.89
notes: Versus waitlist g=1.65 (k=9); pre-post g=0.79 (k=13). 33 early studies across health behaviours. Possible decline effect: 2020 estimates 0.89-1.65 versus 0.15 in the 2025 mental-health meta-analysis (different outcome domains, so not a like-for-like comparison). Xu 2023 (PMID 37521518): pre-post g=0.77 (0.32-1.22), 592 participants, all pre-post designs.

evidence: No pooled estimate located
notes: Gap. Searches G14 and G27 returned no meta-analysis pooling micro-randomised trial effects. JITAI reviews note inconsistent definitions, decision rules and limited optimisation (von Lutzow 2025; Xi 2026).

topic: Aggregated N-of-1 trials of stimulants in paediatric ADHD
evidence: Meta-analyses were consistently in favor of amphetamine in 10 of 11 ADHD symptom domains and methylphenidate in 7 of 12 symptom domains
notes: No single pooled effect in abstract (es null); rater not stated. 9 amphetamine and 10 methylphenidate N-of-1 studies. High heterogeneity of individual response. Companion paper (PMID 27060386): adding N-of-1 data to RCT meta-analyses narrowed CIs in 3 of 4 comparisons. N-of-1 for depression (Kronish 2018, PMID 29596148): only 5 studies, 47 patients, all drugs. No N-of-1 meta-analysis of behavioural strategies found.

topic: Reinforcement learning, Bayesian optimisation and adaptive platform trials for personalising behavioural treatment
outcome: Clinical or behavioural outcome of algorithm-personalised treatment
evidence: researchers tend to use Deep Q-Network (DQN) and Actor-Critic ... to train and validate RL models on retrospective datasets
notes: Gap. No meta-analysis of prospective outcomes. The one systematic review found (40 papers, non-communicable disease) reports RL models trained and validated on retrospective data, with safety and interpretability unresolved. Searches G27, G28 and G34 found no review of Bayesian optimisation or adaptive platform trials in psychiatry or ADHD; depression platform trials appear as protocols or design papers (e.g. Gold 2026, PMID 42742617).

topic: Machine-learning prediction of treatment response, emotional disorders
evidence: The overall mean prediction accuracy was 0.76 (95 % CI: 0.74-0.78), and the mean area under the curve was 0.80
notes: Mean AUC 0.80, sensitivity 0.73, specificity 0.75. Sample sizes 16 to 77,371 (median 175; full text). Higher accuracy with neuroimaging predictors, with larger responder rates, and when outcome imbalance was NOT corrected, which points to inflated accuracy. Abstract says more robust cross-validation gave higher accuracy.

topic: MRI-based prediction of antidepressant treatment response
evidence: overall area under the bivariate summary receiver operating curve of 0.84 (95% CI 0.81-0.87), sensitivity of 77% (95% CI 71-82)
notes: Sensitivity 77% (71-82), specificity 79% (73-84); 22 samples, about 44 patients each. Authors: not ready for practice, external validation needed. EEG equivalent (Watts 2022, PMID 35961967, 15 studies, n=758): accuracy 83.93% (78.90-89.29), AUC 0.850, several models without separate training and testing sets. Resting-state connectivity (Meinke 2024, PMID 38548002, 13 studies): balanced accuracy 77% (72-83) with high risk of bias in all studies.

topic: External validity of treatment-outcome prediction (schizophrenia trials)
outcome: Antipsychotic outcome prediction in independent trials
evidence: Models predicted patient outcomes with high accuracy within the trial in which the model was developed but performed no better than chance when applied out-of-sample
notes: No numeric estimate in abstract (es null). Several independent antipsychotic trials; pooling trials to predict the left-out trial did not help. The reference replication test for precision psychiatry: within-trial accuracy does not transfer. ADHD-specific: polygenic scores did not predict methylphenidate response in 1000 cases from three countries (Rovaris 2026, PMID 41655471).

evidence: In Phase I we find AI-discovered molecules have an 80-90% success rate, substantially higher than historic industry averages
notes: Reported as a range 80-90%; es holds the lower bound. Descriptive analysis of AI-native biotech pipelines, not a meta-analysis.

evidence: In Phase II the success rate is ∼40%, albeit on a limited sample size, comparable to historic industry averages
notes: Approximate ('about 40%'), limited sample, comparable to historic averages: no evidence yet that AI improves efficacy-stage success.

topic: AI-enabled therapeutic assets: Phase 2 success (129 assets)
evidence: The observed probability of success was 77.8% for Phase 1 and 19.5% for Phase 2
notes: Cross-sectional analysis to 1 March 2026: 129 assets, 69 companies, 57.3% oncology; 72 completed Phase 1, 24 completed Phase 2, only five entered or completed Phase 3. Phase 1 success 77.8%. Phase 2 estimate is about half the 2024 figure (about 40%) with a larger sample and different definitions. n is assets, not participants.

outcome: Share of computational repurposing predictions confirmed in trials
evidence: There appears to be an association between clinician-prescribed ketamine and higher remission rates in patients with amphetamine-type stimulant use disorders
notes: Gap. No meta-analysis of how often AI repurposing predictions are confirmed. Validation is typically retrospective corroboration in health records: the cited example (AI-predicted ketamine for stimulant use disorder) reports HR 1.58 (1.15-2.17) for remission in an observational cohort, not a trial. Reviews of validation strategies (Pillai 2023, PMID 38222367; Chen 2026, PMID 42432671) are narrative.

topic: Computational psychiatry: reliability of model parameters
evidence: generally poor for the parameter estimates of the reinforcement learning models (with ICCs ranging from .02 to .52 for the bandit task
notes: No meta-analysis of computational-model validity found; es null because source reports ranges: ICC .02-.52 (bandit, N=69) and .01-.71 (reversal learning, N=47), versus .67-.93 for personality and cognitive measures. Mood explained part of within-person variability. Conflicting single study (Mkrtchian 2023, PMID 38774643, N=50, two weeks): good reliability for learning rates, excellent for loss aversion. Reliability depends on task and model.

topic: Automation bias with generative AI in healthcare
comparison: clinician+AI given wrong advice vs right advice
evidence: recurrent themes included automation bias (reported in 10 studies), concerns regarding clinician deskilling (9 studies)
notes: Gap. No pooled estimate from 2015 onward of how much erroneous AI advice degrades clinician accuracy; recent reviews are thematic. The older landmark (Goddard 2012, PMID 21685142, 74 studies) gives no number in its abstract. Single RCT (Qazi 2026 preprint, PPR1245291, 72 physicians, half of vignettes with deliberate LLM errors): an accuracy-cue nudge raised diagnostic reasoning scores by 7.6 points (1.4-13.9). Non-LLM imaging AI: assisted radiologists' nodule sensitivity RR 1.39 (1.08-1.79), I2 95%, false positives numerically higher in 4 of 5 studies (Singh 2026, PMID 42930660).

evidence: prediction markets can determine the outcomes of direct replications with 73% accuracy (n = 103)
notes: Pooled data from four forecasting projects, 103 findings. Market prices and survey beliefs correlate with outcomes (0.581 and 0.564). Later large-scale work (Mody 2026 preprint, PPR1343191, 37 high-power replications): AUC 0.76 for both Replication Markets and repliCATS, accuracy 73% and 68%. COVID-19 preprint claims: accuracy only 0.57-0.58 (Marcoci 2025, PMID 39706868). Statistical model without humans: 70% cross-validated, 71% in preregistered out-of-sample test, AUC 0.73 (Altmejd 2019, PMID 31805105).

topic: LLMs vs human experts predicting neuroscience results
outcome: Correct choice of real vs altered result (BrainBench), %
evidence: Every LLM outperformed human experts on BrainBench with LLMs averaging 81.4% accuracy and human experts averaging 63.4%
notes: Full text: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC11860209/fullTextXML . 171 experts retained. Task is choosing between an original and an altered abstract, so this is recognition of the plausible result, not open-ended forecasting. LLM confidence tracked correctness. Abstract contains no numbers.

topic: LLM prediction of social-science experiment effects
outcome: Correlation between GPT-4-simulated and actual treatment effects
evidence: Predictions derived from GPT-4 ... were strongly correlated with actual treatment effects, achieving accuracy similar to pooled human forecasts
notes: r=0.85 is from web summaries of the authors' working paper (Stanford project page https://ai4pb.stanford.edu/projects/predicting-results-of-social-science-experiments-using-large-language-models), not from the Nature abstract, which gives no coefficient. 70 preregistered US survey experiments, 469 effects, 119,330 participants. Abstract: predictions 'systematically overestimated effect sizes'; in 15 megastudies (606 effects) correlations were lower but comparable to pooled expert forecasters.

topic: LLM-simulated participants: replication of published experiments
outcome: Share of published main effects reproduced by LLM samples, %
evidence: replication rates for main effects (73-81%)
notes: Other source (arXiv:2409.00128 v3, 20 Jun 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00128), abstract read via fetch tool. Range 73-81% across GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, DeepSeek v3; es is the lower bound. Interaction effects 46-63%. LLM effect sizes about 2-3 times larger than human ones (Fisher z). Where the original study found a null, LLMs gave a significant result in 68-83% of cases. Lower replication for race, gender and ethics topics. No meta-analysis of LLM-human correspondence was found.

topic: LLM-simulated survey respondents: economic preferences in 74 countries
outcome: Share of cultural-dimension associations with correct direction, %
evidence: but only 48.1% (95% CI, (45.1%, 51.2%)) of cultural dimensions
notes: 20 LLM configurations vs 67,201 matched human respondents. Direction recovered for 77.8% (71.6-83.1) of gender, age and cognitive-ability associations but 48.1% of cultural ones. Individual-level alignment 'systematic but modest'; weaker in less developed, less connected countries. Authors: not yet reliable proxies for representative surveys. Bisbee 2024 (Political Analysis, doi 10.1017/pan.2024.5, seen only via secondary summaries): similar means but too little variation, about 48% of regression coefficients differ from human data.

outcome: Agreement of simulated with own survey answers (interview + survey agent), %
evidence: combining them reached 72.8%, compared with 79.5% for participants' two-week test-retest agreement
notes: Other source (arXiv:2411.10109, current version, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10109), abstract read via fetch tool. Demographic-prompt-only simulation 60.4%; interview-based 69.4%; survey-based 69.3%; human two-week test-retest 79.5%. Demographic prompting 'distorts sample-level patterns'; individual data closed a median 53.5% of distortion gaps.

topic: Generative-AI simulated patients for clinical training
evidence: history taking and information gathering (Hedges' g=0.85, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.38--1.32)
notes: Preprint (Research Square); learners are health-professions students; mix of randomized and non-randomized comparisons, so design label is approximate; assessor blinding not stated. Communication/empathy g=1.03 (0.15-1.91); OSCE global g=0.77 (0.09-1.46); clinical reasoning g=0.93 (-0.03 to 1.90). 157 studies, 79.6% published after 2025; mostly short-term, single-site; little evidence on retention or transfer to practice. Fidelity review (Li 2026, PMID 41481915, 39 studies): hallucination rate 0.31%-5%, evaluations with 10-50 students.

topic: LLM-simulated clinicians or therapists (as stand-ins for clinician judgement)
evidence: No pooled estimate located
notes: Gap. Searches G10, G11, G24 and G32 found reviews of simulated patients only. No systematic review quantifies how well LLM-simulated clinicians reproduce real clinicians' decisions. Nearest evidence: LLM vs clinician diagnostic comparisons (generative AI accuracy rows) and an LLM-as-therapist audit reporting stigma and inappropriate responses (Moore 2025, arXiv:2504.18412, no numbers in abstract).

topic: Safety and harms of generative-AI mental health chatbots
evidence: Documented safety failures included missed suicidal ideation and provision of inaccurate clinical information
notes: Gap. No pooled harm rate. Scoping review of 21 studies: human oversight limited, crisis protocols mostly underdeveloped, adverse-event monitoring sparse. Only 3 of 22 chatbot RCTs actively ascertained harms (Yang 2026, PMID 42113705). Preregistered benchmark (Kalinich 2026 preprint, PPR1279036; 49 LLMs, 1.4M inferences on real psychotherapy transcripts): suicidal-ideation detection declined with conversational depth in every model family while clinician performance stayed stable. Systematic review of 8 studies: diagnostic accuracy and cultural competence of generative AI in mental health 'remain limited' (Wang 2025, PMID 40373033).
